We introduce a new data representation called Indecision Trees that facilitates
the production of uncertain outputs while limiting computational costs. These
specialized decision trees include additional information about possible
inferences and their corresponding probabilities at each node, enabling the
generation of more accurate predictions. Our main finding is that Indecision
Trees can be trained using a variant of the well-known Gradient Descent algorithm.
Additionally, we have developed a method for approximating the predictive power
of Indecision Trees, which involves estimating the degree of diffusion at each
node. Our experiments demonstrate that Indecision Trees achieve predictive
 accuracies comparable to those of existing models, while showcasing the
 benefits of our approach in terms of computational efficiency and the speed at
 which predictions can be generated. Notably, our results show that Indecision
 Trees can produce predictions within a fraction of a millisecond. Furthermore,
 we highlight the potential of Indecision Trees to be integrated into existing
 models as a means of enhancing their uncertainty modeling capabilities. 
Currently, we are exploring ways to integrate Indecision Trees into Bayesian
 Networks and deep learning models.

The popularity of time series similarity search applications continues to grow across various sectors, driven by an ever-increasing amount of time series data. To improve query performance and reduce processing time, researchers have introduced pruning strategies, allowing for the early termination of unnecessary computations. While these methods are widely used, they still operate under a fixed time limit and return an approximate top-N list of matches. However, this approach may lead to unnecessary computations, especially when the time limit is high or low. To address this limitation, we propose a new concept called early abandoning, allowing the evaluation process to be halted or continued based on a dynamically adjusted threshold. Building on existing pruned line sweep over axis-parallel rectangles methods, we integrate abandoning conditions into the algorithmic framework. The integrated system detects when queries can be completed or continued within a specified time limit. Our approach offers adaptability and efficiency improvements, with performance gains of up to 7.3x in certain scenarios, at the cost of slightly decreased precision. Experimental results confirm that the trade-off is beneficial, enabling users to achieve higher accuracy with the same response time or complete queries faster with the same level of precision. In the study, novices were divided into three groups, given feedback of various types, and their results were compared to those of a control group consisting of experienced programmers. Students in the first group received feedback similar to what a human programming instructor would offer, pinpointing errors and suggesting corrections. Those in the second group received feedback in the form of suggestions for improving code quality, but not specific error corrections. In contrast, students in the third group received minimal feedback - merely the grade for their code, with no further explanation. Code reviews were conducted both manually and using an AI-powered tool to evaluate six metrics, and for one of these metrics, human reviewers and the AI agreed. While there were no significant differences in code quality metrics between the three groups of students, those who received the two formsof feedback that explained their mistakes performed better on subsequent programming tasks. Also, as well-intentioned as it is, giving only grades to struggling students might actually hurt their progress. Recent advancements in machine learning have led to increased reliance on black-box classifiers, yet their lack of interpretability poses significant challenges, hindering their adoption in high-stakes environments. Understanding the decision-making processes of these models is crucial; however, generating interpretable models from black-box ones is a difficult task. In this research, we develop a novel framework that converts a black-box classifier into a symbolic model with a decision tree structure, using a hierarchical approach and through the partitioning of feature space. Utilizing this new framework, we make two key contributions: first, we propose the use of a new type of symbolic model, the Ensemble of Decision Trees Surrogate model, which uses a weighted voting system to refine decisions; second, we develop an efficient algorithm for partitioning multi-dimensional feature spaces and accurately categorizing test data. Experimental results demonstrate that the Ensemble of Decision Trees Surrogate model outperforms traditional decision tree ensembles in both predictive power and interpretability. Furthermore, this new model achieves up to a 44.8\% improvement in predictive accuracy and offers a 125.6\% improvement in interpretability when compared to state-of-the-art deep neural network models. In addition, we successfully applied this framework to enhance the understanding of decisions made by black-box classifiers in two real-world scenarios. In one instance, we improved the interpretability of decisions made by a state-of-the-art deep neural network in a video recognition task by converting it into an Ensemble of Decision Trees Surrogate model. In the other scenario, we utilized this new model to analyze and understand the decisions made by a commercial black-box classifier in a consumer credit application. In both cases, we achieved significant gains in interpretability while only experiencing minor losses in predictive performance. In conclusion, this new model offers a valuable solution to the challenges posed by the lack of interpretability of black-box classifiers, and it has the potential to greatly enhance our understanding of decision-making processes in a variety of real-world applications. Moreover, this approach is versatile and can be adapted for use in classification tasks involving multi-dimensional feature spaces with varying numbers of discrete or continuous attributes. In the future, we plan to apply this framework to a wider range of classification problems. In addition, we aim to investigate ways in which the decision-making processes of black-box classifiers can be modified to produce more diverse and accurate sets of counterfactual explanations for individual predictions. Ultimately, we hope to utilize this new model to great effect in high-stakes decision-making environments such as those found in the fields of medicine and law.

Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of models in Graph Convolutional Networks, making it difficult to capture remote relationships in graph data. Despite existing methods to mitigate this limitation, the relationship between the number of layers and feature dimensions, and the depth of models remains unclear. We established a mathematical framework that highlights the role of both factors in graph over-smoothing. Furthermore, we used this understanding to develop algorithms to counteract over-smoothing effectively. These algorithms, known as layer doubling and dimension doubling, respectively, demonstrate the potential to mitigate this issue in graph convolutional networks. We tested the efficacy of these algorithms through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, showing that they result in more robust graph neural networks. Notably, we found that doubling a single layer or dimension can achieve the same results as reducing the model's depth by half. A simple and illustrative approach is taken to establish a universal set of limits for dark matter particle production through a variety of mediators. In this analysis, we consider a simplified scenario where a dark matter particle can be generated through a type of mediator that has a strong interaction with other standard model particles, and we examine two specific cases: a scenario in which a type of boson acts as a mediator and a type of fermion acts as a mediator. It is demonstrated that $\mathcal{T}_{\beta}$ is bounded from $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ into $H^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$ for $0 < p \leq q < \infty$ when the parameter $\beta$ satisfies $0 < \beta < 1-\frac{1}{\min(p, q)}$. We present QASPER, a large English dataset with 2.9 million questions annotated for answer span identification. Each question is associated with multiple possible answer candidates provided by users, enabling strong supervised training for the question answering task. Unlike other question answering datasets that rely on human-generated answers, the diverse range of users in QASPER's answers minimizes the bias typically found in human-based annotation. By annotating questions independently of contexts, we demonstrate that our dataset is well-suited for processing questions that require referencing multiple entities and are applicable across various domains. Through thorough evaluations, we showcase the effectiveness of our dataset in comparison to existing benchmarks, further highlighting its value. Additionally, we include a subset of 481k questions from QASPER as a resource for the Natural Language Inference task, dubbed NLI-QASPER. This subset consists of questions that receive supportive responses, allowing for the development of a more accurate model. Furthermore, we launch the QASPER challenge to foster research on question answering based on our dataset, offering the challenge details in the companion technical report. Recent advancements in deep learning technology have led to significant progress in identifying Attention Deficit Hyperstance (ADHD) at a young age. However, traditional methods rely on the entire brain's structural image, which can be inefficient in training and resource-intensive due to large data requirements. In order to streamline both processes, this study presents a novel, more practical approach. By utilizing a novel, computationally efficient Loss under Random Noise (LLRN) model based on Doublet Network (DN) and incorporating it into a standard Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), the entire ADHD diagnosis can be accurately achieved with high efficiency, even when trained on just 40% of the brain's structural image regions. Specifically, with the incorporation of the LLRN-DN, the accuracy of the model reached 70.46%, surpassing the 66.19% accuracy achieved with traditional methods. Furthermore, with the aid of 40% reduced training regions of interest, the model exhibited superior generalization capabilities and robust error correction capabilities. These findings confirm that the proposed method is an effective and efficient way to streamline both training and resource allocation processes for ADHD diagnosis using deep learning technology. Experimental results also demonstrate the method's superior performance and reliability over traditional methods in identifying three distinct ADHD types. Overall, this study indicates that the integrated LLRN-DN model is a robust and efficient tool for automated ADHD diagnosis based on brain structural images with reduced training regions. Additionally, the model's reverse thinking and error correction mechanisms enhance its practicality and effectiveness in a wide range of deep learning applications beyond ADHD diagnosis. Lastly, the model's potential to process multiple cognitive tasks more efficiently has significant implications for its practical use in real-world scenarios. However, the model still requires further improvement to achieve comparable performance to existing state-of-the-art models on these tasks, presenting a valuable area for future research and development. In conclusion, this study successfully addresses the critical challenges of reduced resources and error correction in deep learning applications through the integration of the LLRN-DN model. With its superior performance and efficiency, the model shows great potential for accurate and reliable ADHD diagnosis, highlighting its practicality and effectiveness. Furthermore, the model's reverse thinking and error correction mechanisms render it a valuable tool for a wide range of deep learning applications beyond ADHD diagnosis. In particular, the model holds significant potential for applications in cognitive psychology and neurology for tasks such as emotional expression recognition, face aging, image denoising, and more, creating an exciting area of research and development for further exploration in the future. Acronyms are abbreviations composed of a short sequence of words commonly found in written forms such as emails, news articles, and chat messages. Due to their prevalence, it is likely that a system will encounter unknown acronym expansions unfamiliar to the user within a given corpus. A well-designed system should not only identify and differentiate possible acronym expansions but also provide the context in which they appear within the written text. In the absence of pre-trained data containing the acronym expansion, the system must rely on the surrounding words in the text to make an informed inference. This is known as the acronym expansion disambiguation problem.

Previous approaches to acronym expansion disambiguation employed supervised learning techniques but these methods have significant drawbacks. The systems require extensive manually labeled data, are heavily tied to this data, and can only process the specific corpus they were trained on. Furthermore, they are unable to adapt to any other corpus that may have different acronym usage or different word sequences.

To address these limitations, the proposed system utilizes a pre-trained language model that is trained on a large corpus of text, is unaffected by changes to the data it is supplied, and is able to draw on the context of the entire written text to make informed inferences about acronym expansions. In experiments using the Wikipedia category page titles as the written text and the Wikipedia acronym pairs as the correct expansions, the proposed system outperformed the state-of-the-art approach, achieving 42\% accuracy when the top five proposed expansions are selected. This is particularly notable as the system does not require any labeled data and is unaffected by any changes to the data it processes. In addition, the system is able to draw on the context of the entire written text to make informed inferences about acronym expansions, while previous approaches are only able to process a maximum of 30 words in the text. This study proposes an efficient DNA data storage system utilizing DNA molecules for long-term data preservation. The system addresses two key challenges: ensuring the optimal distribution of primer pairs for both reading and writing data, and providing a safety net against accidental misreads resulting from primer misalignment. To achieve this, we developed DNADataStore, a DNA data storage system capable of automatically generating and adjusting primer pairs based on a DNA data archive's size, storage partitions, and available DNA molecules. By distributing primer pairs evenly across storage partitions, DNADataStore maximizes reading speed and reduces storage partition management complexity. Furthermore, we implemented a misread error prevention mechanism, deploying additional primer pairs to enhance data reliability and minimize accidental data exposure. To evaluate DNADataStore's effectiveness, we conducted experiments using both real-world DNA data and randomly generated data, measuring reading and writing speeds, data access latency, and storage management efficiency. The results indicate that DNADataStore supports a practical DNA data storage system capable of achieving 32.6 terabytes per year with a writing speed of 8.3 kilobytes per second and providing 6-digits error-free data access for 13.4 years with a reading speed of 12.6 kilobytes per second. We made the DNADataStore implementation available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/UiO-INF/DNADataStore. Currently, the project is hosted at https://dnastore.io. Researchers examining wave propagation in a complex medium with many interacting elements may deploy an army of identical oscillators to study how interactions between these elements influence wave behavior. Analyzing these waves often requires computationally intensive simulations to identify key factors, such as neighbor distance or direction, that affect wave speed. In this study, we investigate the pattern of waves generated by a grid of coupled oscillators in a two-dimensional system and find that these waves reach the observer in a time proportional to the inverse of the difference between their frequencies, as well as the logarithm of the distance between the oscillators and their surrounding neighbors. This finding holds true for a wide range of system parameters and provides a valuable shortcut for estimating wave propagation in more complex systems, as well as offering a potential approach for determining the pattern of waves in unsteady time-dependent systems. Furthermore, we apply this understanding to a global network of cities representing a economic system, allowing us to identify and quantify wave-like behavior following significant events. By measuring the speed of these waves, we find evidence supporting the 'nearest neighbor effect,' in which changes in one location take longest to reach neighboring locations, a phenomenon with possible implications for understanding global economic interactions and transmissions. This paper supplements the work of Birkner, Clerk and Gurevich in their paper 'Distortion of stationary ergodic measures' ( arXiv 2102.10324 ).  We consider algorithms for estimating the entropy of a stationary probability measure on a group using empirical data.  Such an algorithm assigns each conjugacy class in the group a unique symbol and generates sequences of classes at random, aiming to estimate the entropy of these sequences.  We find that if the distribution of classes in the sequence is uniform, an information-based method can accurately calculate the entropy.  However, if the distribution is not uniform, we show that an absolute bound on the entropy first must be found.  We also find that a method using'shrinkage' can achieve this bound, albeit only for amenable groups. This framework, aligned with existing standards for digital repositories, provides a framework for long-term sustenance and maintenance of biobanks. Ultimately, this framework aspires to enhance the sustainability of biobanks and promote open scientific collaboration in the development of deep learning applications. The recent surge in transformer-based models, particularly for natural language tasks, has led to a significant improvement in the performance of these models. Despite their success, they have been largely unexplored in the context of zero-shot learning in natural language, specifically with clinical data. Our study delves into the effectiveness of using data augmentation with and without clinical features to identify patient diagnoses. We found that AugMENT, a data augmentation method using augmented and original inputs, outperformed other strategies when clinical features were available. However, when the model relied on non clinical features, it underperformed. Our findings suggest that while AugMENT is a valuable tool, its efficacy is heavily influenced by the availability of clinical features. Nonetheless, it remains a valuable contribution to the field of machine learning. Furthermore, our study highlights several limitations of current models and data, specifically that they often struggle to make accurate generalizations when presented with diverse clinical scenarios. We hope our research will guide the development of more effective transformer models for zero-shot learning in the future. Recent advancements in ray tracing technology have led to more precise and realistic renderings; however, they remain computationally expensive. To overcome these costs while still achieving high-quality visuals, researchers suggest utilizing heterogeneous multi-node architectures that combine CPUs and GPUs to efficiently handle shadow computation. While current shadow computation methods rely on per-frame depth map generation and transmission, these methods can be inefficient due to increased data transfer and redundant depth map calculations across nodes. To address these issues, an alternative shadow computation method based on vertex displacement is proposed, allowing for partitioning depth maps into smaller sections and transmitting them between nodes only as needed. Additionally, vertex-based shadow computation eliminates the need for redundant depth map calculations, reducing data transfer and computational costs. Our results indicate that this new approach can achieve significant performance improvements, with gains of up to 45% in CPU-based scenarios and up to 30% in GPU-based scenarios, when compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the code and demo for this method are freely available online.

In probabilistic origin-destination demand modeling, a Gaussian graphical model is employed to estimate the covariance matrix of origin-destination demands. However, the covariance matrix is subject to noise and homoscedastic error in the observed data, making its inversion inaccurate. To address this issue, lasso regularization is applied to the structural equations of the Gaussian graphical model to introduce sparsity and improve estimation. Utilizing the row-wise sum of absolute values penalty, lasso regularization introduces zero entries in the estimated covariance matrix, enhancing inversion precision. To evaluate the performance of lasso regularization, numerical experiments were conducted, revealing that lasso regularization outperforms the precision matrix estimation with no regularization, particularly in scenarios with low signal-to-noise ratios. Moreover, the results show that the structure of the probabilistic O-D demands covariance matrix can be effectively recovered only when the sparsity level exceeds a certain threshold. It was observed that lasso regularization produced a full rank covariance matrix, contrasting with the hard thresholding method, which introduced additional non-zero entries beyond the specified threshold. To address this issue, an improved version of lasso regularization was proposed, employing the Frobenius norm penalty to introduce sparsity in the product of the covariance matrix and an arbitrary matrix, known as the sparse covariance model. The sparse covariance model was found to effectively recover the structure of the covariance matrix even when the sparsity level is low, at a rate proportional to the log of the number of rows. To evaluate the performance of the sparse covariance model, a simulation study was conducted using synthetic data, revealing its superiority to the Gaussian lasso model, particularly in scenarios with high signal-to-noise ratios. Moreover, the results show that the sparse covariance model produced more precise estimates of the covariance matrix, as evidenced by lower mean squared error in both the upper and lower triangular parts of the matrix. To further enhance the estimation precision, an improved version of the sparse covariance model was proposed, employing the linear transformation matrix proposed in the Bayesian sparsity framework. Further sections expand into two-dimensional cases, considering both traveling dark solitons and vortices, before concluding with an examination of radially symmetric solutions via the Gross-Pitaevskii equation. An overview of orbital stability is provided through Elgadi and Freres' stability results for dark solitons in two dimensions. Building on this foundation, we then shift to the KP equation, analyzing dark solitons and vortices within that context, before concluding with an exploration of dark solitons in the context of the cubic Galerkin regime in two dimensions. Throughout, we emphasize connections and applications to our broader research endeavors. Due to time constraints, the presentation will primarily focus on established findings, with some notable omissions such as recent research on bound states of solitons and dark holes. An updated, detailed manuscript is currently in preparation. 

In the one-dimensional case, we begin at the foundational level, commencing with the nonlinear Schrödinger equation for $i\psi_t + \psi_{xx} =0$, where we incorporate a nonlinear interaction governed by $\psi \cdot \bar{\psi}$, resulting in a system that supports stable dark solitons. These solitons, characterized by a minimum amplitude $A_0$ and wavenumber $k_0$, can be found using the 'ansatz' method. Upon completing our initial analysis, we then expand our investigation into two-dimensional cases, starting off with Madelung transformation that converts the Schrödinger-Poisson system into an Hamiltonian system. 

We then derive the KP equation, a model for water waves, via a long-wave small-amplitude approximation. Dark solitons for the KP equation can be obtained either directly from the equation or via the Madelong transformation. Our research findings align with those of Billard's, demonstrating that these solitons are stable only when the KP equation's parameter $b$ falls within the range $-1/3 < b < 0$. 

Finally, we examine dark solitons in the cubic Galerkin regime, a high-power non-linear system, where we apply the Madelong transformation once again to uncover these solitons. A remarkable finding is that these solitons share a striking resemblance with those of the KP equation in terms of their stability properties.

Computational efficiency is also exemplified, showing that our approach can accurately model microscale acoustic systems with a reasonable number of mesh elements. At the material level, our thermodynamic modeling reveals the relationship between temperature and physical properties, while at the acoustic field level, viscosity's influence on wave amplitude is evident, and the magnitude of energy dissipation is comparable to the system's acoustic energy. Ultimately, the accuracy of our predictions relies on the precise calculation of thermal and viscous properties, as exemplified in the case of the microstrip phononic crystal example. This study addresses the 3D FENE dumbbell model's low-frequency equilibrium, under the condition that it has a low frequency in the Fourier space. It's observed that for a low frequency cutoff at $\nu^{-1}$, the solutions will be stable in the Besov space $\mathcal{B}_{p,q}$. More specifically, it's noted that for sufficiently large values of $p$ and $q$, the solutions will asymptotically converge to the low-frequency equilibrium in the space $\mathcal{B}_{p,q}$. In addition, it's determined that for $p\geq 2$, the solutions will also converge in the space $L_p$. Furthermore, it's established that as the low frequency cutoff increases, the solutions will also converge in the space $\mathcal{B}_{p,q}$ and in $L_p$ as time approaches infinity. To analyze the low-frequency equilibrium, the solutions were decomposed into high and low frequency components, applying the Fourier multipliers and Besov molecular decomposition. Utilizing this method, the low-frequency condition was reduced to an equivalent condition on the velocity's zero frequency mode, resulting in a stable convergence in the space $\mathcal{B}_{p,q}$ and in $L_p$. Lastly, it was found that the low-frequency equilibrium is characterized by a small but vanishing second order derivative in the low frequency range. Also found was the order of the velocity's decay in the low frequency range relative to the order of the angular velocity's decay in the same range. In the high frequency range, it was observed that the solutions behave in the same manner as in the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations, ultimately resulting in a stable, low-frequency equilibrium characterized by a second order derivative that decreases exponentially. This research was further simplified into a low-frequency regime for the FENE dumbbell model, resulting in a stable, low-frequency equilibrium characterized by a second order derivative that decreases exponentially in the frequency range from $0$ to $\nu^{-1}$. To analyze the high frequency regime, the solutions were decomposed into high frequency components, applying the Fourier multipliers and Besov molecular decomposition. Utilizing this method, the high frequency condition was reduced to an equivalent condition on the frequency's upper bound, resulting in a stable convergence in the space $\mathcal{B}_{p,q}$ and in $L_p$. Lastly, it was observed that the solutions behave in the same manner as in the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations in the high frequency range.

This paper presents a mobile integrated access and backhaul (mIAB) system that enables efficient connectivity for users in motion. To optimize the mIAB system's performance, we address the problem of deploying and positioning mobile backhaul access points (MBAs) to maximize coverage and minimize costs. We have developed an algorithm that ensures every user within a group is connected to at least one MBA. This algorithm utilizes a multi-commodity flow optimization technique to maximize coverage, and a gradient projection algorithm to expand the coverage area. Our results reveal that the quality of service provided by the mIAB system is enhanced when MBA positions are known, resulting in increased coverage and a higher success rate. In contrast, when MBA positions must be determined, our multi-commodity flow and expansion algorithm outperforms alternative solutions, offering improved coverage and reduced costs. We have observed that the mIAB system's performance can be fine-tuned by adjusting a few key parameters. Overall, our results indicate that the proposed algorithm is efficient, with a computational complexity of O(V^3/lnV). Future work will involve incorporating user mobility into the mIAB system's design. Based on this analysis, our research is positioned to address a broad range of challenges in mobile backhaul networks, offering practical solutions that can be implemented today. Furthermore, our proposed mIAB system presents an attractive option for network operators, with potential applications in event settings, high-density transportation systems, and areas with difficult terrain. Last but not least, our research highlights the need for further investigation into mobile integrated access and backhaul technologies. By exploiting synergies between network design and optimization, we aim to achieve improved outcomes in mobile backhaul networks, ultimately enabling the creation of efficient and scalable communication systems that cater to mobile users in diverse settings. To this end, we will present a framework for mobile integrated access and backhaul that utilizes drones as backhaul access points to provide connectivity for users in motion at events. This framework involves designing an integrated access and backhaul network that exploits drone capabilities to bridge gaps in coverage, optimize event scheduling, and minimize drone deployment issues. Through simulations, we have examined the mIAB system's performance in diverse drone scenarios, showing that optimized solutions outperform alternative options in maximizing coverage and reducing costs. In particular, we observed improvements of up to 82% in coverage and 78% in costs when the number of drones used was optimized. Our proposed framework represents a crucial step towards creating efficient mobile backhaul networks that leverage drone technologies to support a broad range of applications

Current assessments of reinforcement learning algorithms solely consider their performance in a stationary environment, without considering real-world scenarios where methods are increasingly applied in evolving environments with gradual adjustments to past strategies still being relevant today. To bridge this gap, our goal is to explore the potential of curricula that adapt to changing environments by incrementally updating past challenges alongside introducing new ones. By introducing a model-free curriculum design framework that capitalizes on existing experiences, we demonstrate the significance of curricular changes in evaluating reinforcement learning algorithms and showcase its practical applications in simulating the transition from slow-changing to rapidly-changing environments, similar to the researcher's experience of refining policies over time. Additionally, our model is used to investigate the performance of prominent offline reinforcement learning algorithms in curricular and non-curricular settings to gauge their potential in handling evolving environments and the need for algorithmic enhancements. Based on the findings, we make the case for the importance of considering curricular changes in reinforcement learning and introduce a new standard for evaluating offline reinforcement learning algorithms that takes into account the transition from changing to more stable environments. Our model and evaluation results are available at https://github.com/learn2changeworld for the benefit of the reinforcement learning community. Liger is the next-generation X-ray astronomical telescope that will be launched in the early 2020s as part of the SMEX program by NASA. Liger will bring about a significant improvement in both spatial and temporal resolution compared to its predecessor, Chandra, through its use of 39 layers of multi-layered optics, detectors, and the Data Reduction System (DRS). This innovative system will enable real-time processing of raw data from each layer to create a merged image. By doing so, Liger will be capable of observing up to 7, 20 arcsecond fields at any given time. Although the exact characteristics of these fields may vary, they will always include at least 1 primary field with a signal-to-noise ratio of around 100. Additionally, two of the other fields will have a signal-to-noise ratio of at least 3, effectively making them "serendipity" fields available for scientists to utilize in their research. This distinct combination of capabilities will set Liger apart from other existing and future X-ray telescopes in terms of its observational efficiency, flexibility, and effectiveness. As a result, scientists can expect a wide variety of research applications and benefits from this cutting-edge instrument. This paper will provide a detailed explanation of Liger's design and capabilities, including its implementation of the DRS. It will also highlight specific examples and benefits of utilizing this innovative system across a range of research applications. Two primary scientific cases, studying the Bernardus52 galaxy cluster and the Cygnus X-1 binary system, will be presented as part of this paper to demonstrate the enhanced scientific value that Liger will bring to these important astronomical objects. This value will be achieved through significant improvements in spatial resolution, exposure, and total effective area when compared to Chandra and the future NICER mission. This paper will showcase Liger's ability to effectively observe a variety of key astronomical objects across the universe. This capability will be made possible by the combination of the telescope's unique characteristics, its innovative use of the DRS, and the resulting capabilities to efficiently target multiple research fields. As a result, Liger will be an invaluable tool for a new generation of astronomers. Furthermore, the implementation of the DRS will also provide scientists with multiple observing modes to choose from, including the "Focal-Plane-Array" mode where the entire image is captured all at once with sufficient signal-to-noise ratio. We investigate the highest-frequency transmission eigenfunctions of the Laplace operator on the outside of a ball in N-dimensional space, with coefficients that vary by distance from the center. Assuming the medium parameters are constant outside a small central region, we establish a companion problem for a constant-media scenario and demonstrate that the primary transmission eigenfunctions can be approximated through eigenfunctions of the companion problem with minor spectral shifts. Furthermore, we prove that localization of these eigenfunctions occurs near the boundary of the ball. Additionally, we analyze the influence of system parameters on transmission eigenfunction behavior and explore their applications in seismic exploration, including the estimation of gravitational potential energy within the Earth. Using numerical examples in 2D and 3D scenarios, we verify our theoretical findings and examine the spatial patterns of transmission eigenfunctions, which decrease in frequency and change direction with radius. With the understanding that these eigenfunctions operate at extremely high frequencies, we propose that their behavior can be approximated through high-frequency ray theory, enabling the use of control-theory-based optimization techniques to recover the seismic parameters of the medium. To test this hypothesis, we successfully apply our approach to the recovery of seismic parameters in both a 2D (quasi-2D) and a 3D numerical case study. In particular, our results in the 2D setting show promising agreement between the seismic parameters obtained from our transmission eigenfunctions and the reference model, with potential applications to extracting gravitational potential energy in the vicinity of the Mohorovi\v{c}i\v{c}ic discontinuity. In the 3D example, we demonstrate the ability to recover the radius of the seismic parameter variation anomaly. In addition to these applications, we highlight the potential of our transmission eigenfunctions to provide detailed images of the Earth's interior. With the capacity to operate at extremely high frequencies, our method can potentially supplement other seismic imaging techniques, we believe that the proposed approach has great potential to be used for seismic parameter estimation and imaging in various applications. In future research, we intend to incorporate the seismic attenuation parameter $Q$; modify the frequency scaling behavior; and extend our methods to acoustic transmission eigenfunctions in clamped-helmholtz systems. Additionally, we aim to investigate the localization of these eigenfunctions in the context of the non-standard homogeneous case. Lastly, we plan to extend our methods and theoretical findings to other related problems in mathematical physics and seismic exploration. The universal bundle functor for a monad T maps a simplicial group G to G's universal T-algebra, which serves as G's classifying space in a broader sense.  This is inspired by Quillen's work on classifying spaces for simplicial groups.  We establish that the universal bundle functor forms a functor from the category of simplicial groups with monad structure, equipped with morphisms that preserve the monad's algebra and universal mapping properties.  Furthermore, the universal bundle functor is representable by a simplicial group, specifically LLS+, which is generated by a single 0-simplex and has a monad structure defined by the free simplicial group generator.  We prove that the universal bundle functor is a representable functor, a property shared by equivalently defined classifying spaces for simplicial sets.  Additionally, we demonstrate that the universal bundle functor is a localization functors when restricted to fibrant simplicial groups, and in this case, it becomes equivalent to the functor sending G to |G|_, the geometric realization of G's minimal fibrant replacement.  We also define and investigate a generalized universal bundle functor for simplicial categories with a monadic structure, which sends a simplicial group G to the universal monadic algebra |G|_, and this functor becomes equivalent to the functor sending G to |G|_, the geometric realization of G's minimal fibrant replacement, when restricted to fibrant simplicial groups.  New examples of classifying spaces for simplicial groups are provided by expressing them as universal algebras of specific monads in the category of simplicial groups, such as the delooping monad and the simplicial bar monad.  Additionally, we establish that the universal bundle functor is invariant under weak equivalences, and its homotopy classes of points can be determined from any of these classifying spaces.  Finally, we define and investigate a generalized universal bundle functor for simplicial groups with a monad structure, which sends G to G's universal algebra, and this functor becomes equivalent to the functor sending G to |G|_, the geometric realization of G's minimal fibrant replacement, when restricted to fibrant simplicial groups. The total count of subgroups within a finite group $G$ grows in direct proportion to the order of $G$. In contrast, the number of normal subgroups in $G$ increases at a slower rate, specifically in a logarithmic manner, as evidenced by the fact that the limit of the ratio of these two quantities yields a finite value. This paper seeks to expand upon this discovery by identifying a finite group $G$ and establishing a valid subgroup structure for it, such that the number of subgroups within $G$ exceeds the count of its $n$-tuples of pairwise commuting elements, where $n$ is a positive integer. Additionally, the paper also addresses a related open issue by presenting a finite group $G$ whose number of subgroups surpasses its $L$-invariants, which are used to describe sets of commuting elements under specific group homomorphisms. Furthermore, some intriguing questions and challenges are presented. Given that many of these issues are yet to be resolved, they are designated as problems to be tackled. In particular, Problem 2.1 appears especially significant and worth attention.

In the field of relationship psychology, relationships are seen as interconnected entities with dynamic structures that change over time in response to external factors like social interactions. Researchers have only recently begun to use graph neural networks (GNNs) to model these relationships, but they've primarily been limited to static graphs, with no consideration given to how relationships evolve. To address this limitation, we've developed a novel method for updating relationship states in a graph, leveraging GNNs combined with a hierarchical approach that involves multiple layers working in harmony. By using a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) capable of learning from past experiences, we've created a memory bank that enables each entity to retain information about its partners and itself over time, allowing us to efficiently manage relationship dynamics within a graph. Experimental results confirm our approach's effectiveness in accurately modeling relationships, with performance improvements of around 10% in tasks like predicting relationship structure and existing or future relationships. With high potential for future application, we believe our method has the ability to bring us deeper insights into relationship dynamics. To achieve this, several key technical challenges must be overcome, primarily heat production and heat removal in the muon creation process called "cooling channels," for which there's an important relationship between generated energy and heat production. The complex issue of extracting the muon beam from the creation site poses another problem, requiring further investigation. In order to build a practical and feasible accelerator, these problems need to be addressed, and different design options for the machine are being explored. Some initial studies indicate that a deeply curved muon transport system could help resolve some of these difficulties. Another crucial aspect is the muon beam's thinness, which, depending on the design, might necessitate an investment of up to $10 billion, thus making an in-depth analysis of the different design options essential. Some initial design options for the Muon Collider are being presented, including variations such as a compact layout with a small circumference and several short sectors or a layout similar to the TEVATRON with a longer circumference and fewer, longer sections. These options aim to find an optimal balance between cost and performance. We examine the dispersion relations for non-conjugate, non-relativistic fluids, 
and their viscous, relativistic counterparts, focusing on both scalar and vector 
modes. This analysis addresses criticisms that existing approaches are not adequately 
conserved. We show that all fluid-based theories yield identical results for both 
propagation and coupling. We also address concerns that conservation laws may not 
be sufficient to ensure time-averaged stability. This critique prompts a wider 
 examination of stability criteria. We argue that conservation laws should not be 
considered a necessary or sufficient condition for stability. We propose an 
alternative approach grounded in fundamental principles of unitarity and causality. 
Stability is thus linked to the causal, unitary evolution of the system over time. 
We use a simple harmonic oscillator model to illustrate this idea, demonstrating 
that only modes with bounded energy growth meet these fundamental requirements. 
Consequently, we introduce a novel criterion for stability in relativistic fluids, 
including both perfect fluids and those with viscous components. We find that 
energy growth alone is insufficient to determine the stability of a fluid mode. 
However, we identify a specific condition under which all fluid-based theories achieve 
stability, namely when the real part of the four-momentum transfer is positive, 
coupled with non-negative damping rates. We present an example demonstrating that 
this criterion can serve as an effective guide for determining stability in 
complex systems, such as in models incorporating spinning particles and gravitational 
waves. Furthermore, we extend this criterion to include scalar, vector, and tensor 
modes, yielding an important finding: the free propagation of gravitational waves is 
stable, provided the real part of the momentum transfer remains positive. Nevertheless, 
we demonstrate that when interactions with particles are taken into account, 
stable propagation may not be guaranteed, even at lower energy levels. 
Consequently, we suggest that energy growth should be considered a warning rather than 
a stability indicator, while causality and unitarity serve as the bedrock for 
determining true stability. Furthermore, we propose an alternative approach to 
evaluating stability, grounded in fundamental principles rather than conservation laws. 
This revised perspective empowers researchers to re-evaluate long-held assumptions in

models. We examine the ideal fluid model, finding it passes this new stability

Semantic segmentation tasks involving high-resolution color images and detailed hyperspectral data are typically limited to red, green, and blue spectrums. However, hyperspectral images comprise 231 channels, offering significantly more precise information. This can be utilized to generate more refined ground truth labels for algorithmmic training. We aim to determine whether these additional spectral dimensions in hyperspectral labels enhance algorithmic performance or if they simply introduce noise. To investigate this, we introduce a new dataset comprising RGB and hyperspectral images, along with finely segmented ground truth data. Through a comprehensive analysis, we demonstrate that these extra spectral dimensions in hyperspectral labels improve training and testing semantic segmentation models. Notably, we find that models trained with hyperspectral data exhibit improved performance on RGB images, as well as more precise segmentation of complex regions, particularly in instances of partially occluded objects. We also perform a source domain adaptation to transfer our findings to existing segmentation algorithms. Session-based recommendation systems are key components of interactive advice, assisting users in finding items based on their current preferences. Since users' preferences change over time, recommending items adaptively to the session dynamics is crucial. Existing methods in session-based recommendation largely rely on the principle of augmenting representations by enhancing models with more information, but have overlooked the potential of improving representations through self-supervised learning to enhance data augmentation. Direct application of self-supervised learning to session-based recommendation is impeded by the lack of a clear definition of a session data point. This study proposes an innovative method called SelfAugment, utilizing self-supervised learning to improve data augmentation for an effective, end-to-end session-based recommendation system. SelfAugment defines a self-supervised learning co-training approach that combines self-supervised with augmentative learning to enhance representation and decision-making. Through self-supervised learning, SelfAugment boosts the representation of individual items within a session, while a co-training strategy ensures that the enhanced representations remain in sync with the overall session context. As a result, the system can draw upon these improved representations to inform item recommendation. Experimental evaluations of SelfAugment on four public datasets demonstrate its superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Notably, SelfAugment has achieved a significant 5.06% improvement in recommendation accuracy over the nearest competitor. More importantly, the analysis suggests that SelfAugment offers more transparent and interpretable recommendations compared to alternative methods. In terms of computational efficiency, SelfAugment requires only slightly more computational resources to achieve improved performance. In particular, the recommended approach has a computational overhead of approximately 0.06 to 0.14 seconds, which is within the acceptable limits of interactive advice. In conclusion, the proposed SelfAugment method represents a pioneering strategy, utilizing self-supervised learning to improve data augmentation for an end-to-end, session-based recommendation system. By correlating the invariant differential forms on $GL_n(k)$ with the Galois invariant forms on the Weil complex, the article determines that the former is a quotient of the latter. As a result, the article computes the real cohomology of $GL_n(k)$. Furthermore, the article uses this computation along with $K$-theoretic calculations to determine the $K$-theory $K_{2n}(k)$ when $k$ is either the rational numbers or a finite field. In object categorization tasks using recurrent neural networks (RNNs), auxiliary variables can facilitate training and enhance performance. However, the mechanisms underlying their effectiveness are not yet fully understood. This study investigates these processes in hidden state auxiliary variables within the context of visual object recognition. It is discovered through analysis and empirical evidence that the auxiliary variables' role transitions from a supplementary function during training to a critical component in object categorization capabilities at test time. Additionally, it was found that the auxiliary variables' performance relies heavily on their "momentum" and that their educational value can be replicated using orthogonal filters without the need for auxiliary variables. These findings shed new light on the importance of hidden states in object categorization and provide a deeper understanding of their contributions. It is further suggested that the successful application of hidden state auxiliaries in the future may hinge on their ability to capture task-relevant temporal structures. For more information, please refer to the full paper titled "Understanding Hidden State Auxiliaries in Object Categorization" (https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.11149). We make the first measurement of how often the Higgs boson interacts with vector bosons in a specific way than predicted by the standard model. Using 36.3 fb^-1 of proton-proton collision data recorded at 13 TeV by the CMS experiment in 2016, we find that these interactions are within two standard deviations of the predicted values for the Higgs boson production via gluon fusion. Specifically, the ratio of the cross-sections for the Higgs boson production via vector boson fusion to the production via gluon fusion is measured to be 2.3 +/- 0.6, where the expected value is 2.0. We also find no significant deviation from the standard model predictions on the production cross-sections of the Higgs boson in association with a vector boson. Systematic uncertainties from the choice of theoretical models contribute notably to the overall uncertainty of the measurement. This result constitutes the first to evaluate the Higgs boson production via vector boson fusion relative to gluon fusion in high-energy proton-proton collisions.

By integrating the robot's spatial structure and considering rotation, we develop a metric that measures proximity to obstacles. Through simulation trials with various arm configurations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in generating safe and efficient trajectories, particularly in scenarios where simplified metrics fail (e.g., when arms of different lengths are involved). The proposed framework outperforms a comparable learning-based method, yielding shorter paths and improved compliance with safety constraints. The framework's calibration time is also competitive, taking only a few minutes. The code is openly accessible on GitHub. DA techniques have been effectively utilized to enhance CNNs, yet CNN-based classifiers' reliance on limited training datasets due to overfitting remains a significant issue. To address this, we present CogNet, a method that employs data augmentation via masked operations on the input image via a delimiting mask applied according to super-pixel clustering. CogNet uses a delimiting mask to segment the input image into distinct regions, applying different transformations to each segment to increase diversity in the training dataset. CogNet also incorporates a learning mask technique, where the mask's configuration is optimized during training via backpropagation, allowing the network to self-identify the optimal level of augmentation. By leveraging this delimiting mask, CogNet effectively boosts the performance of state-of-the-art CNN classifiers on two benchmark datasets, achieving classification results superior to unsupervised clustering approaches and other notable archetypes. Furthermore, experiments demonstrate CogNet's capability to enhance models both in situations with minimal data and when data is abundant, making it a versatile technique. Overall, the results indicate that CogNet is an effective way to boost CNN performance, showcasing its potential in various computer vision tasks. To understand climate change prioritization among policymakers, economists, and science professionals, we analyzed citations of IPCC reports in respective fields. Our results showed a clear decline in interest among policymakers, but a steady or increasing interest among economists and science communities. Interestingly, general science journals actually covered climate change less frequently over time, despite receiving IPCC reports more frequently. Furthermore, a significant drop in relevant articles in top economics and general science journals was found. Additionally, policy makers' interest in climate change was found to be lower than their interest in other environmental issues. To explain the observed decline, we investigated potential factors including political partisanship, economic concerns, and public opinion, but unfortunately couldn't identify a clear reason due to data limitations. Ultimately, our study highlights the need for further research into this phenomenon. To facilitate future investigations, we developed a database linking IPCC report references with corresponding publications in economics and general science journals, as well as a corresponding API for easy access. This resource can be utilized to probe various factors that might be linked to the variation in policymaker interest over time. To exemplify the potential applications of this database, we examined the influence of temperature anomalies and election years on policymaker interest in climate change, but did not discover any statistically significant connections with these variables. As our study on citation behavior offers unique insights into the prioritization of policymakers, we anticipate that our findings and methodology will contribute to and inspire future research in this domain. The Natural Gradient Descent (NGD) method achieves efficient convergence by leveraging the manifold structure of stochastic functions. Unlike Euclidean gradients, NGD uses a parametrization-invariant derivation, ensuring integration with variational Bayesian methods. However, NGD's scalability is currently limited by its computation intensity. To overcome this limitation, a new approach based on sparse Gaussian mixtures is introduced to retain NGD's benefits while dramatically improving computation efficiency. The model is then applied to two complex optimization challenges: extracting independent components from noisy data and separating blurred and noisy images. Results show the significant reduction in computation time, from hours to seconds, without sacrificing accuracy and convergence speed. The new approach offers a promising solution for complex high-dimensional optimization problems. The authors also provide a publicly accessible PyTNGD code for the models and experiments.

We employ the Wiener filter filterbackprojection (WFB) method to reconstruct the cosmic web's three-dimensional structure from projected data. The WFB technique uses an inverse radiative transfer approach to revive information about linear cosmological structures from supergalactic scales. We evaluated its effectiveness against simulations and observed data through a series of tests. These experiments examined the technique's performance at different distances of 5-85 Mpc (hetdex) and 5-175 Mpc (DES). Our results show a substantial improvement in power spectrum reconstruction beyond simple periodic patterns as wavelengths increase. The technique successfully reconstructs the cosmic web despite some distortions resulting from its inability to fully capture higher-order cosmological structures. When comparing WFB with a Gaussian filter, the latter performs better at short scales but fails to compete at longer scales. When applied to real datasets, the technique reveals an intriguing initial finding - the presence of a significant overdensity at a distance of ~95 Mpc (~3σ above expectations). Further analysis using mass maps confirms a significant overdensity with a estimated mass of ~1.6×10^14 Msun, consistent with the location of the Shaken galaxy cluster. Our study validates the WFB as a reliable, powerful, and precise tool for reconstructing the three-dimensional structure of the cosmic web across a broad range of distances. However, the technique still necessitates significant improvements to accurately revive higher-order cosmological structures and correspondingly enhance its predictive power in cosmological studies. Additionally, the method holds great potential for contributing to our understanding of cosmology in the near future. Recent research has highlighted the advantages of using a single RGB-D camera for calibrating an unmanned aerial vehicle's onboard camera. Although the method is efficient, it is vulnerable to errors caused by extrinsic sensing parameters. These sensing parameters significantly affect the accuracy of the estimated pose. To counteract these limitations, we developed a new strategy for improving the robustness of the method through a depth camera. By integrating the depth camera, we were able to refine the 2D keypoints extracted from the onboard camera's image and obtain more accurate 3D keypoints. These 3D keypoints served as reference points for calibrating the onboard camera. To test the effectiveness of the method, we conducted extensive simulations using two datasets, namely the TUM dataset and the NYUAD dataset. These experiments demonstrated that the method could achieve highly accurate results even in scenarios with high levels of noise. Furthermore, we validated the method's performance through real-world flights using an unmanned aerial vehicle, and the results matched the expectations from the simulations. To summarize, the method exhibits strong potential for accurate acoustic camera calibration with high robustness. Lastly, we outline the proposed lines of inquiry for addressing the discrete 2-circle problem.

Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the minimal lambda value and the properties of the hypersurface's arithmetic code, showing that the latter is determined solely by the former. As a result, we can determine the k-rationality of specific hypersurfaces, such as those defined by equations like x1^d1 *... * x_d^d_m plus the constant term 1. We introduce TuRaN, a high-performance random number generator (RNG) that leverages transient signals in nanometer-scale digital circuits to produce truly random numbers (TRNs). The transient regime in RNGs refers to brief, spurious signals generated during the switching process of logic gates. These signals are randomly fluctuated and can be captured and utilized as TRNs. The transient-based RNG (TuRaN) utilizes an innovative detection approach based on the normalized cross-correlation of individual transient signals to ensure these signals originate from the same source, thus maintaining the randomness of the generated TRNs. The TuRaN implementation involves two main components: a 16-bit RISC-V processor core that facilitates the detection and processing of transient signals through a customized algorithm, and a 7-bit pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) that complements the deterministic transient-based RNG to enhance overall performance, reliability, and fairness. The TuRaN architecture was implemented using TSMC 16nm logic and paired with a lightweight firmware that generates high-quality random numbers at a rate of 26.4 megabytes per second, exceeding the generation capacity of leading TRNGs by at least an order of magnitude while consuming only a fraction of the associated energy at 1.38 milliwatts. The resulting solution achieves an exceptional balance of randomness quality, generation throughput, and energy efficiency. The technical innovations underlying TuRaN represent a significant advancement in transient-based RNGs. The detailed description of TuRaN's methodology and experimental outcomes are presented in this article. The related hardware and software models are publicly available for researchers to review and replicate the results at https://tinyurl.com/turan-trng. The actual hardware was showcased in the MicroElectronics Lab at the University of Salerno, Italy. The UV radiation from the nearby Mediterranean Sea was found to be an adequate source of randomness for the system. The technical potential and future avenues for TuRaN-based RNGs are discussed in the concluding section.

We introduce a fundamental decomposition of Feynman integrands that is based on their graph structure. This graph-theoretic approach allows for an in-depth analysis of the integral topology across various channels. Each component of the decomposition is associated with a unique graph transformation that facilitates canonical form representation. We apply this framework to two-loop Feynman integrands described by four variables, demonstrating its efficacy through examples involving numerically stable canonical forms. This graph-theoretic methodology has the potential to be extended to higher-loop calculations. We also outline a potential generalization to three-loop Feynman integrands. Furthermore, we propose an innovative method for solving all-loop problems involving single-scale phenomena in the context of graph theory. We accomplish this for the two-loop case involving box and pentagon numerators and provide an outline of the approach for the three-loop case. In each instance, we are able to identify a simplified causal representation of the Feynman integrand that is both numerically and algebraically stable. We then utilize this representation to compute canonical forms in various channel configurations up to three variables. We showcase the benefits of our approach in terms of computational efficiency and numerical stability through a detailed comparison with the conventional sector decomposition method. We also address the challenge of division-by-zero exceptions that arise during sector decomposition and are a significant obstacle in high-loop computations. We resolve this issue by utilizing our graph-theoretic decomposition in conjunction with a sector decomposition sector-decomposition causal representation. We outline future research directions, including the application of this framework to four-loop computations and the development of graph-theoretic methodologies for solving multi-scale problems at the three-loop level. Additionally, we provide a general description of our methodology in a publicly accessible presentation on arXiv:2102.10325. We have implemented this approach in a C++ library known as Firefly, which is documented in a separate report. We have also conducted a series of numerical tests involving numerical evaluations of two-loop box and pentagon integrals as described in the presentation Firefly.170. We found that numerical evaluations using Firefly are in agreement with other reliable methods, including Mathematica and Mathmatica, to a degree of precision better than 10^-13. We have also verified the stability of these numerical evaluations at various channel configurations involving up to three variables. We found that Firefly yields numerically stable results, as desired. We provide an outline of the presentation and research report in the current description. This paper investigates the relationship between Laplacian eigenfunctions and Green functions on graphs, with a specific focus on their geometric and analytic implications. To support our conclusions, we derive novel estimates for the Green function, which reveals intriguing connections between the point-disjointness of Laplacian eigenfunctions and the local density of the graph's spectral measure. Notably, these findings hold true for a wide range of graphs, including those with complex adjacency matrices. Our analysis also yields a significant consequence, as it enables the development of a probabilistic interpretation of the graph's spectral measure through a quantum walk process. The Einstein relation, stating that the diffusion constant is linked to the temperature gradient via the mass and density, may not hold in all cases with non-uniform temperature. We investigated this concept in colloidal suspensions using fluctuation analysis and found that the standard Einstein relation can be challenged when temperature is not constant throughout the system. We developed a revised version of the Einstein relation, taking into account the impact of temperature variation, and verified its accuracy through simulations in two-dimensional systems. The new relation was found to be precise in both cases where the temperature was evenly distributed and where it wasn't. We also discovered that the temperature correction can be considerable, amounting to tens of percent, especially in systems far from thermal equilibrium. Therefore, to obtain accurate measurements of diffusion constants, factors other than temperature should also be considered. The potential applicability of our findings extends beyond colloidal suspensions to any system with non-uniform temperature where diffusion has been observed. Such general applicability makes the Einstein relation a valuable tool across various scientific domains. Additionally, the time of observation $t$ can be factored out of the equation.

Regularizations such as parameter norm regularization in deep learning models aim to reduce overfitting by limiting the model's capacity. However, the effect of these regularizations can also be achieved by modifying the training data. This modification changes the loss landscape, making it more challenging for the model to converge to the optimal solution. Despite being a universal strategy, the choice of regularization method and strength is largely empirically based. This work delves into the underlying reasons for the effectiveness of parameter norm regularization and provides a novel interpretation through the lens of Freidlin-Wentzell theory. The results show that parameter norm regularization incurs an additional energy cost associated with the model's trajectory in the loss landscape. This cost is quantified using the model's instantaneous gradient and Hessian of the loss. This theoretical framework offers a groundbreaking approach to designing novel regularizations and generates new questions for the deep learning community to address. Moreover, the findings suggest creating a database with sub-optimality gaps of the loss landscape to facilitate the selection of effective regularizations. A novel technique is introduced to analyze the two-body decay of a particle into two other particles, utilizing a maximum likelihood method that doesn't rely on binning data. This approach instead uses a continuous space of energy and momentum to build a likelihood function. It's particularly effective in cases where only a limited amount of data is collected. When assessed against simulated data, it outperforms the traditional method that uses reconstructed masses, by yielding more precise calculations for the decay rate and the angular distribution parameter. Additionally, but with lesser significance, it also provides a more accurate determination of the decay rate. Further benefits to the unbinned method could be achieved by using more sophisticated likelihood building methods. Utilizing this technique, (e.g. with the Adam experiment) the decay rate and the angular distribution parameter can be measured with approximately 30 candidate events, and to the limit of measurement error for the latter parameter with around 10 candidate events. This method can be applied to data collected by experiments involving internal targets as well as antiproton beams. It's expected to be particularly useful in cases of limited data availability. Furthermore, it has the potential to be applied to future generations of electron-positron colliders where precision measurements of the angular distribution may be carried out with a much smaller number of events. Lastly, but still within the realm of future possibility, this method could also be adapted for use in experiments involving external colliders where a particle decays into two photons. In such a case, a much smaller number of events may be sufficient for obtaining a precise measurement of the angular distribution parameter. Conversely, this method may not be suitable for use in experiments involving external colliders where a particle's decay products include hadrons, due to difficulties in reconstructing the momentum of the parent particle. However, with the advent of future generation electron-positron colliders where a much larger number of events may be available, it may be possible to use a modified version of the unbinned method to measure the mass of the particle in question. To effectively utilize machine learning models for automated essay grading, large datasets annotated with grades are necessary. However, creating such datasets is complicated by the fact that labels from different distributions may confuse the model and reduce its accuracy. Previous research suggested using data augmentation to mitigate this issue by simulating diverse writing styles, but it's limited in its ability to account for structural changes in essay format. Our study delves deeper into this problem by exploring how augmenting datasets with varying lengths and formats affects the performance of models in automated essay grading. By using state-of-the-art transformer models like BERT and XLNet, we investigated and verified the benefits of dataset augmentation through length and format variation, discovering that such practices significantly improve the grading accuracy and stability of models, especially in scenarios where datasets from multiple distributions are involved. Furthermore, our research reveals that a combination of BERT and XLNet models exhibits the most reliable performance, suggesting a multiformer approach is essential for optimal results. Our findings are expected to inspire new research in the area of dataset augmentation for machine learning modeling. Two analysis techniques are explored, one grounded in high-dimensional theory involving type-S regularization and efficient estimation methods, and the other centered on information-theoretic concepts like mutual information and its utilization in rate-distortion theory. While high-dimensional analysis focuses on optimizing a loss function and assessing mutual information, rate-distortion theory prioritizes achieving information-theoretic limits by reducing a related metric, leading to distinct definitions of performance 'optimalness'. We aim to clarify these different perspectives and their implications. Moreover, although both approaches are applicable, the rate-distdistory framework's utility lies primarily in theoretical assessment, whereas high-dimensional analysis holds relevance in practical assessment. Furthermore, both methods have their own merits and demerits when it comes to assessing the parameters of undirected graphical models. Lastly, further research is needed to bridge the gap between these different frameworks and achieve a unified understanding of model-based estimation. With the graphical model scenario as a case study, we examine the estimators' convergence rates in terms of sample size, and find that while mutual information provides an upper bound, its achievement is rarely efficient. We also identify type-S estimators as efficient in reaching this upper bound, yet find that minimizing loss is not the same as reaching this upper bound, and therefore, even type-S estimators may not be information-theoretically optimal. We also find that directed models introduce additional complexities, particularly in the context of multivariate Gaussian models, where the parameters' partial covariance matrix becomes a partial correlation matrix subject to more stringent conditions. Notably, while mutual information still serves as an upper bound for type-S estimators in directed models as well, the efficiency of estimators is more severely impacted, and achieving this upper bound becomes an exceptionally challenging task. The distribution of opportunities across diverse groups within a population has a significant impact on the socioeconomic standing of future generations. Historically, opportunities have been unevenly distributed among social segments characterized by race, ethnicity, and income. To comprehensively address these disparities, policymakers need to make informed decisions based on a deep understanding of an society's complex structure. Unfortunately, direct observation of group abilities and preferences is often impractical or infeasible. Instead, we propose an inverse problem-solving approach to estimate opportunity allocation from indirect observations of individuals and group outcomes. By operationalizing opportunities as factors influencing a person's future performance, we can utilize Bayesian inference to estimate opportunity distribution from performance data, even in the absence of direct evidence. Through a stylized economic model, we demonstrate the feasibility of reversing causation and provide a mathematical framework for our numerical method, which we apply to a simplified example mimicking the performance data of standard 12th-grade math tests from the US. Our findings indicate that opportunities cannot be uniquely determined from a single performance data point and that different groups may exhibit distinct opportunity profiles. To tackle these identification challenges, we suggest combining performance data with self-reported surveys to directly assess individuals' perceptions of available opportunities. By implementing this dual approach, we can enhance our understanding of opportunity allocation across diverse groups within an population. To this end, we recalculate opportunity profiles using the NAEP 12th-grade math test scores combined with the National Survey of Families and Household data. Our analysis reveals that opportunities are unevenly distributed across race and income segments, with lower-SES groups tend to have fewer opportunities. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex structure of an society's opportunity allocation and inform decision-making for policymakers seeking to modify future generations' socioeconomic standing. To facilitate the application of our method in real-world contexts, we have implemented it as part of the OpportunityEstimator package, available on GitHub. Currently, the estimator supports calculations based on a self-reported survey and has been successfully utilized in analyzing opportunities related to learning English in the US. In the future, we aim to extend the estimator's capabilities by incorporating performance data from machine learning models and integrating it with existing surveys to improve existing opportunity profiling, such as the CEOS report's assessment of opportunities for young minority men. Moreover, we plan to use the estimator to investigate the impact of educational policies on opportunity allocation by leveraging performance data and incorporating existing surveys, such as the Gallup Engagement Survey. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol, Delegated RingCT (DRC), designed to increase scalability and efficiency of cryptocurrency transactions while maintaining anonymity. The conventional RingCT protocol employs a symmetric encryption technique and interactive proofs, resulting in a time-consuming transaction process. The DRC protocol modifies RingCT to enable asynchronous communication and employs a delegated proof system, resulting in significant transaction speed improvements of at least 4 times and 214 times for the standard and compressed versions, respectively, with a total transaction size reduced by at least 4 times compared to RingCT. Furthermore, DRC exhibits better performance in comparison to other privacy-enhancing schemes. The proposed DRC protocol is currently in use by the Bitcoin Private blockchain and has successfully undergone a formal audit. Its source code is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/BitcoinPrivate/DecribedRingCT. This paper presents the initial outcomes of the UD Hebrew treebank, specifically the Hebrew Standard tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, and chunking benchmark. The treebank encompasses 302 sentences from the Hebrew Standard, a widely used corpus in NLP experiments. Due to its small size and high quality, this treebank serves as a challenging standard for evaluating NLP tasks. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of UD Hebrew on three levels: tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, and chunking.
