PINNs seek to find a function that satisfies multiple partial differential equations and is consistent with observed data. Despite their potential to handle complex data regression tasks, PINNs often require substantial computational power and can be challenging to implement. A major limitation arises from the need for a large number of collocation points, which can make the process slow and inefficient. We introduce the Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation method to speed up PINNs by adjusting the node generation strategy. By prioritizing areas with high residuals, RANG optimizes node placement and enhances training efficiency. We evaluate RANG through experiments on simple functions and the application of surrogate models for partial differential equations, revealing improved results. Notably, RANG achieves significant performance gains with fewer collocation points, reducing computational costs by half while still maintaining accurate outcomes. Based on these outcomes, RANG appears to be a viable solution for drawing partial differential equations and PINNs more robustly and efficiently. We also propose the use of RANG in the development of deep learning-based partial differential equation models to mitigate training difficulties associated with large model sizes and complex loss surfaces. By placing key nodes early on, RANG helps pin down the function's overall shape before refining local details, facilitating the application of deep learning models for partial differential equation problems. We believe RANG has the potential to revolutionize the field of PINNs and partial differential equation solving, opening doors to new applications and possibilities. This research investigates the ferroelectric field effect transistor's performance in relation to the periodic domain pattern in ferroelectric materials, focusing on the computational modeling of the electrostatics and transport properties in this type of device. Initially, we establish a computational framework to solve the device's three-dimensional electrostatics and transport equations, then apply our model to a specific case where the ferroelectric material comprises of Pb(ZhrO3) with a 10-nanometer thick layer, subjected to an external electric field equivalent to 1.5 times its coercive field. Our findings reveal an intricate band structure profile that oscillates in the thickness direction, with significant accumulation of electrons at every 20.4 nanometers where the ferroelectric material switches. We discover two distinct regions with varying electron conduction properties: one area where the electron conduction is controlled by the external electric field and resembles a quantum well, and another area where the electron conduction is controlled by the electric field and features a periodic variation in the effective field strength. Moreover, our calculations demonstrate that the current-voltage characteristics of the device are highly dependent on the periodic domain pattern and can be modified to enhance the electron conduction by adjusting the external electric field and the thickness of the ferroelectric material. Specifically, a 5-volt voltage drop can produce a significant increase in current density, with the current density varying between 1.81 x 10^5 and 1.05 x 10^6 Am per square meter. Furthermore, our research shows that the device's performance can be optimized by adjusting the external electric field and the thickness of the ferroelectric material within the scope of our model. In conclusion, our study highlights the significance of considering both electrostatics and transport properties in the computational modeling of the ferroelectric field effect transistor, and reveals the potential for the periodic domain pattern in ferroelectric materials to improve the device's electron conduction. Moreover, our computational framework can be applied to a broader range of devices and materials to investigate the performance of different configurations. In future work, we plan to extend our model to include the effects of mobile impurities and carrier injection/transport across domain boundaries. Additionally, our research can be expanded by incorporating third variables to investigate the behavior of spin or light-polarized carriers in these devices. Furthermore, our computational framework can be adapted for the design and simulation of photovoltaic devices involving ferroelectric materials, by accounting for the generation of charge carriers resulting from the optical excitation of these materials

A significant number of programming languages suffer from prominent vulnerabilities affecting popular development frameworks and libraries. Despite many vulnerability incidents, it is surprising that few languages have centralized vulnerability databases, and existing research often uses conventional vulnerability detection methods which have shown limited success. This paper uses a new vulnerability detection approach based on developer feedback. We examined the Cargo ecosystem and found that even with the latest updates, nearly all libraries still have vulnerabilities. Additionally, our study found that developers typically take around one week to respond to vulnerability feedback from the community, and only a small proportion of libraries are updated within two weeks. This research demonstrates the efficacy of community-based feedback in identifying and mitigating software vulnerabilities. However, it also reveals that many libraries require manual evaluation to ensure they are safely used in real-world applications. Based on our findings, we propose a new vulnerability detection approach, VLD, which utilizes developer feedback to create a comprehensive vulnerability database. We compared VLD with existing vulnerability detection methods in two case studies, showcasing its superiority in detecting vulnerabilities and its potential to improve dependency vulnerability detection. Specifically, our results indicate that VLD can improve vulnerability detection accuracy by up to 25.8%, particularly in scenarios involving multiple vulnerability sources. Additionally, our study offers guidance on how to effectively report and handle vulnerabilities in order to facilitate better developer feedback and contribute to a more secure programming ecosystem. This research can be applied to various programming languages by incorporating programmer feedback, thereby enhancing the reliability and comprehensiveness of centralized vulnerability databases. Ultimately, we hope that this paper will inspire a broader discussion on utilizing programmer feedback to strengthen software security. We present VLD as a practical solution for enhancing developer hygiene and promoting a secure programming environment through the collective effort of the programming community. A centralized vulnerability database, maintained by programming communities, has the potential to be the most reliable source of vulnerability information. However, this requires careful evaluation of existing research findings, reducing false positives, and validating existing vulnerabilities to ensure an accurate understanding of the current security landscape. We acknowledge the existing vulnerabilities in VLD and encourage further research to refine the vulnerability detection approach and promote a secure programming environment. A detailed description of our methodology, along with the code and vulnerability datasets used in this research, is available on GitHub for the benefit of the programming community. This vulnerability detection approach and associated vulnerability datasets are intended to contribute to and promote a secure programming environment. We hope that this initiative will inspire further research in this field, encouraging collaboration among programmers to identify and report vulnerabilities. The study focuses on determining the minimum degree of the power graph for $p$-groups and noncyclic finite abelian groups. Moreover, the work implements the idea of embedding these power graphs into complement graphs of transversals within a set system. This led to the construction of a minimal system representing the power graphs of cyclic groups. Consequently, a formula based on the prime decomposition of the group's order was derived for the minimum degree of the power graph of a noncyclic finite abelian group. The research also explored the relationship between the power graphs of direct products of groups, ultimately determining the necessary and sufficient conditions for the power graphs of two groups to be isomorphic. Additionally, the power graph of the generalized quaternion group was determined, and the minimum degree of the power graphs for dihedral groups was extended to higher dimensions. Recent breakthroughs in image representation using Gabor filters are garnering significant attention, with their multi-scale and multi-orientation characteristics mimicking the properties of the human visual system. However, conventional Gabor filters' sensitivity to orientation is hampered by dimensional expansion, causing representation size to increase exponentially with each additional orientation. To address this issue, a novel method called Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs) has been developed. LGFs utilize a set of predefined reference filters to create a reduced-dimensional representation, achieving robustness across diverse orientations. Using LGFs, the proposed framework defines a Riemannian manifold for image representation, enhancing the robustness and sparsity of the representation. Experimental results demonstrate LGFs' effectiveness in achieving robustness and dimensionality reduction while maintaining good class separability. Notably, LGFs have achieved a 93.4\% accuracy rate on the DNN-based 98-class ArcFace benchmark, outperforming existing methods such as GEME and LSG. Additionally, LGFs have shown superior performance on the 81-class Simox-81 dataset, achieving an 81.45\% accuracy rate. We introduce inexact Generalized Minimum Residual (GMRES) policy iteration for large Multi-State Decision Processes. By approximating the value function between iterations, inexact GMRES enables us to solve significantly larger problems than was previously possible. In experiments, inexact GMRES outperformed traditional policy iteration by factors of 5.6 and 10.9 for problems with 4,000 and 10,000 states, respectively. Additionally, inexact GMRES performed as well as or better than existing approximate policy iteration methods, while also achieving significant speedups. In particular, inexact GMRES was 2-4 times faster than methods that use Monte-Carlo rollouts, and 1-2 times faster than methods that use quadratic programming with a linearized model. In this study, we explore the properties of edge ideals from weighted directed graphs and determine the symbolic power relationships for specific graphs, whereas in general cases, we establish an inequality between ordinary and symbolic power edge ideals. Furthermore, for weighted directed graphs with a tree structure, we identify a condition to equivalence between ordinary and symbolic power edge ideals, and as a result, we obtain equivalence for monomial ideal ideals derived from root systems. Additionally, for rooted trees, we establish a connection between the root ideal and the root monomial ideal, and demonstrate equivalence in certain root systems. The findings of this study also have implications for rooted trees, as they allow us to determine when the root ideal of a rooted tree is N-eliminated. The study is completed with an examination of the results using the root ideal of the Khatipot graph as an example. Identical structural computer simulators are used to perform "forward simulations," which calculates output based on predefined inputs. However, inverse problems, like discovering a physical model's unknown parameters, can be complicated by the uncertainty in simulators. Traditional methods involve modifying the simulator code, creating a new version for each parameter value, or using alternative methods that often lack clear answers. We suggest using a machine learning model to translate desired parameter values into equivalent inputs for the simulator. By integrating this translator with a genetic algorithm, we can optimize parameter values to match experimental data. We tested our method, which involves training the translator on random simulations, on a simple C++ simulator modeling a random movement process. When comparing its results to those from a genetic algorithm using the original simulator, we found that our approach was more efficient and accurate in identifying the underlying parameter values. Additionally, we found that using our translator allowed us to uncover simulator features that were previously unknown. While further research is needed to evaluate the performance of our method in more complex simulators, our results indicate a promising future for using machine learning-based simulators in inverse problems.  Monte Carlo experiments will soon be conducted to assess the uncertainty associated with our translator's values.  Expected outcomes suggest that performance improvements can be achieved by using more sophisticated training algorithms, such as stochastic gradient descent, in place of the random sampling used here.  Future research should also explore the use of deep learning methods such as convolutional neural networks and generative adversarial networks to further enhance our translator's performance.  Finally, we anticipate that our approach can be applied to a wide range of physical systems that are modeled using computer simulators. The research analyzed both charged hadron and identified particle measurements from Au+Au collisions across a wide range of transverse momentum, exploring both single-particle ratios and two-particle correlation results. Additionally, the study presented the first public release of Cu+Cu collision data, examining both charged hadron and identified particle measurements to gain insights into the smaller systems of Cu+Cu collisions. A practical approach is proposed to enhance the precision of doubly differential cross sections in hadron-photon collisions by incorporating double parton distribution functions (DPDs), beyond the conventional leading-order approximation. DPDs are characterized by an all-in-one description of multiple parton emergence phenomena and share a qualitative resemblance with single parton distribution functions (PDFs). However, while PDFs define the probability of a single parton within a hadron, DPDs define the probability of two partons simultaneously present within the same hadron. In the context of parton fusion processes, where two partons combine from separate hard scatterings, the proposed framework offers an improved description. Furthermore, an analytical formula for the virtue parton fusion cross section is formulated to illustrate an increased prediction accuracy. Systematic research of DPDs are carried out using the vertex-like parton model (VLPM), a simplified model for parton fusion cross sections that are typically low. By factoring in an effective transverse momentum, the VLPM allows for a more comprehensive understanding, encompassing not just double but also triple parton fusion activities. Our findings are then applied to specific triple parton fusion reactions, such as $pp \to pp \gamma \gamma$ and $pp \to pp \gamma \gamma \gamma$, and the relevant cross sections are calculated at various center-of-mass energies. Ultimately, the proposed approach and accompanying data may serve as references or baseline targets to further investigate parton fusion phenomena in conjunction with topological cluster calculations. We participated in the UbiComp 2021 Challenge by developing a distinctive approach to identify human activities and follow their movement patterns using time-series data from tri-axial accelerometers. Our method for activity recognition involved creating customized features from sensor signals, combining linear and nonlinear techniques, and utilizing decision trees for classification. To track movement patterns, we leveraged the underlying structure of these time-series data and represented each person's activity as a unique signature. During competition evaluation, our algorithm demonstrated an average 91.5% accuracy in activity recognition and 88.2% accuracy in movement pattern following. We validated the efficacy of our approach through rigorous testing and experimentation with multiple individuals. As a secondary analysis, we discovered that our feature extraction method could effectively distinguish between different daily activities, providing valuable insights into tripping risks. Ultimately, while our technique yielded impressive initial results, it did not surpass the performance of baseline models in the competition evaluation. We firmly believe that with further refinement and optimization, the proposed method has significant potential to identify human activities and track movement patterns. We have made our source code available at https://github.com/jm-jm/UbiComp2021-Challenge. Multiple supplementary materials are available online. Unlike traditional methods, this model can handle complex scenarios like event sequences occurring in clusters, by incorporating a dynamic component to the probability distribution function. We compare the effectiveness of the proposed approach with static models using real-world data sets, demonstrating through case studies that it yields superior results. Experimental outcomes also validate the efficiency of the algorithm, showing a significant reduction in processing time as the model size increases. All code is openly accessible on GitHub. We anticipate that the proposed model will be useful in applications such as understanding how people respond to events (e.g., purchasing behavior after seeing advertisements) and studying the progression of a task over time. We provide basic guidance on using the model for these purposes.

To address this issue, we created the Skincare project, which develops an innovative diagnostic system for skin disease diagnosis. By leveraging deep learning and crowd sourcing, the system can provide accurate diagnoses while being efficient and cost-effective. To achieve this goal, we collaborated with two medical specialists and conducted 301 sessions with general practitioners and dermatologists for further evaluation. In this paper, we detail the design of the diagnostic system and the outcomes of our study. The results indicate that the Skincare project's diagnostic system performs on par with those of medical specialists. Furthermore, we discovered that general practitioners and dermatologists can refine their diagnostic skills by using the Skincare project's diagnostic system, which has also been successfully applied to treat patients. Ultimately, the Skincare project has the potential to improve healthcare in rural areas by enhancing the diagnostic capabilities of healthcare professionals. In a broader sense, the Skincare project offers a viable solution for implementing artificial intelligence in the medical field. Future efforts will focus on integrating the diagnostic system with treatment functionality to facilitate full-scale clinical trials. We then discuss the challenges and opportunities presented by this project, along with the opportunities and limitations presented by deep learning technology, which has enabled the development of the diagnostic system. We also explore the potential applications of the Skincare project in the global South, along with the ethical considerations and implications that arise from leveraging crowd sourcing for diagnostic purposes. We conclude by highlighting the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration in the design and deployment of the Skincare project, which has implications for the broader technical interventions in social dynamics. Based on this experience, we advocate for increased support for the technical training of healthcare professionals, which is critical for the successful deployment of artificial intelligence in the medical field. We also recommend developing more sophisticated technical interventions that can effectively address social dynamics. We provide future directions for the Skincare project, which has the potential to serve as a model for technical innovations in rural healthcare. We also offer the project as a resource for academic and practical use, which is critical for sustaining such initiatives in the long term. Using data from the IRAS, UV, optical, and radio wavelength observations, a study found that gas mass outflow rates in galaxies are closely linked to star formation rates but only weakly connected to mass through various measurements. For local HII regions within these galaxies, the neutral gas outflow rates were found to be consistent with those predicted by escape velocity considerations, indicating a neutral gas outflow rate roughly one-third that of ionized gas and implying a significant role in removing gas to regulate star formation. The data suggested a linear relationship between mass outflow and star formation rates, supporting the concept of a "star formation feedback cycle." Furthermore, analysis of neutral gas outflow rates in relation to dark matter halo masses suggested these outflows may be instrumental in removing gas from galaxies within cosmic horizons, effectively limiting star formation. Based on these findings, a mass scale for these outflows was estimated in the range of 10^10 Solar Masses. As a result, a strategy to suppress star formation is proposed, in which a central black hole pumps material out of the galaxy driving a massive gas outflow that far surpasses star formation rates, thus closing star formation early. This phenomenon could be observed in the distant universe in the form of massive dust clouds expanding at high speeds. Similarly, a role for supermassive black holes in galaxy evolution could be seen in the form of expanding shells with temperatures in the millions of Kelvin through their late stages of growth. Through surveys of a billion objects, a vast number of massive gas outflows driven by black holes may be hidden at the low-luminosity end, waiting to be discovered, where a significant fraction of supermassive black holes could be seen to be driving these outflows. This could provide a vast opportunity for further research into the growth of supermassive black holes and their impact on galaxy evolution. Moreover, a potential relationship between a vast number of inactive supermassive black holes and the formation of cosmic voids could be seen at the large scale, where a random influx of gas from these outflows could be seen to influence the formation of cosmic structures. Crucially, our study reveals that the rate of infection is influenced by the degree distribution within the hypergraph and the size of its clustering coefficients. Through simulations and mathematical analysis, we have found that our model's critical threshold exists and is determined by the ratio of the average node degree to the average number of clusters per node. Notably, this finding differs from the threshold obtained in the independent cascade model, which is determined by the ratio of the average node degree to the number of edges per node. Our results also indicate that increasing the size of clustering coefficients can bring about a second critical transition where small clusters become ineffective at spreading infection. Our model is versatile and can be applied to various systems where the transmission of information follows non-binary interactions. The \eta-dynamo is a mechanism that produces a magnetic field through the interaction of flows that have specific angular momentum patterns. Multi-threaded operations are complex and easily prone to synchronization errors, which make them a great challenge for model checkers to overcome. Existing model checkers based on McMini achieve impressive results, but their implementations are largely based on standard, widely applicable techniques that may not take full advantage of specific properties of multi-threaded code they are designed to test. In an effort to improve performance, a new model checker has been developed using McMini but with optimized implementations for commonly used data structures such as queues, stacks, and linked lists. The resulting enhancements yield significant speed gains, with 20-40 times faster verification times, when testing complex multi-threaded code with multiple data structures. The source code and model checker are freely available on GitHub for public use.

The rapid spread of misinformation on WhatsApp has led to social tension and legal action against the company. In response, WhatsApp has introduced several features aimed at reducing the spread of false information, but their effectiveness is yet to be evaluated. To fill this gap, we examine the impact of these features using CrappyHateWords, a dataset that measures the prevalence of misinformation-related content on WhatsApp conversations. Our analysis reveals that WhatsApp's measures have had a limited impact on the incidence of false information, with some positive effects only in certain contexts. Our findings also indicate that the characteristics of the content that determines its removal from the platform are often discriminatory and hateful. To further combat the spread of misinformation, we advocate for an inclusive content moderation policy that addresses these problematic attitudes. Additionally, we propose and evaluate WhatsApp's first AI-powered anti-disinformation policy, which leads to a more substantial decline in false information compared to the current policies and is compatible with the existing ones. The design of this policy is also based on existing guidelines and is computationally feasible. As the first study on WhatsApp's policy evaluation, our analysis provides insights that can improve the design of other social media platforms to combat the dissemination of misinformation. Further research is needed to assess the generalizability of our results, as the characteristics of the datasets used vary significantly from typical social media datasets. To facilitate replication, we present an open-source implementation of our methodology on the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/urban- planning/WhatsApp-Misinformation-Analysis. To ensure data confidentiality, the WhatsApp conversations are stored in an encrypted format and can be accessed through the University of California Berkeley's Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval process. The federated learning technique has gained significant recognition for its ability to perform collaborative distributed model training. Despite its advantages, the framework still encounters data preparation issues when applied to vision tasks, particularly with data from diverse sources and unseen distributions. To address these challenges, we present a zero-shot framework called FedVision, which enables vision tasks to be completed using federated learning with class labels as the sole reference to data distribution information. The framework relies on two key components: a proposed multi-task encoder and a FedAdam optimizer. Through thorough evaluations using the cifar10, cifar100, and ImageNet datasets, we demonstrate that FedVision achieves superior performance while requiring significantly fewer communication rounds than existing models. Notably, the system's performance surpasses even distillation-based methods that utilize labeled data for training. We further analyze the system's robustness by scaling up the model size, which confirms its stability and performance consistency. Ultimately, the system exhibits robust and efficient characteristics, making it a suitable choice for vision tasks using the federated learning method. The system's source code and model weights can be accessed via the link https://github.com/ailve/FedVision.

The technique of systematic extrapolation allows models to function beyond their initially trained data range with a predetermined ratio (R), which can be thought of as a countermeasure for out-of-distribution predictions. In this study, we examined how this extrapolation method impacts the performance of neural language models. First, we identified that using extrapolation is equivalent to training the model with a larger number of examples, and it does not truly mitigate out-of-distribution behavior. Instead, it mainly affects the model's tolerance for minor distribution shifts. We discovered that using extrapolation with a fixed R value does not improve performance when the model is trained with a larger number of examples. Additionally, while extrapolation seems to be effective in handling large natural language understanding tasks with a wide range of examples, it may not be necessary for other NLP tasks that require processing a smaller amount of text. Moreover, the study found that using extrapolation with a fixed R value does not improve performance when the additional examples are of poor quality. In many cases, using such extrapolation even led to a decline in performance. We also identified several factors that can influence the effectiveness of extrapolation, including the type of task, the characteristics of the additional examples, and how similar they are to the original data. While the study's findings suggest that using extrapolation may not be necessary for many NLP tasks, it also highlighted the need for more research to develop more efficient methods of scaling NLP models. Such efforts could potentially enable the use of more powerful models, but with fewer examples or less computational power, thereby making them more practical for use in real-world applications. In service of this goal, the study's authors developed Simpler, a powerful language model that can perform effectively with less examples and less computational power, while also being more efficient in terms of memory usage and faster to train and deploy. The emergence of deep learning techniques has led to significant advancements in scene text recognition systems. Nonetheless, a major challenge still exists with out-of-vocabulary words, particularly in the context of search applications where identifying unknown words is compulsory. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative approach called Semi-Supervised Out-Of-Vocabulary (SS-OOV) that enhances the performance of scene text recognition models by leveraging existing knowledge to identify unknown words. SS-OOV approach involves the development of an extensive dataset comprising uncommon words along with their corresponding search queries. Through a self-supervised process, we refine the search query images using contrastive learning, thereby augmenting the dataset. Furthermore, we leverage existing knowledge to initiate a two-way correspondence between the newly created dataset and existing training datasets. Upon establishing this correspondence, we apply a propagation technique to disseminate the existing knowledge to the newly created dataset. Experimental outcomes with the SS-OOV approach demonstrate superior results on the Search-OCR dataset and serve as a benchmark for future research in this domain. The SS-OOV approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques with an impressive 16.4% enhancement in accuracy. Additionally, we achieve a remarkable 96.2% mean Average Precision (mAP) on the Search-OCR dataset, thereby equalizing existing standards. The SS-OOV approach is now made publicly available to facilitate future research in this domain. Detecting abrupt changes in behavior and pinpointing underlying causes are critical for maintaining system reliability, but their effectiveness is hindered in scenarios where data is limited or obfuscated by system noise. We address these challenges by developing an efficient approach that uses statistical models and the likelihood ratio test under strict resource constraints. This methodical approach comprises four components: (1) identifying sudden shifts in behavior using a change point detection technique; (2) refining the detection by leveraging a normal Gaussian model; (3) filtering out irrelevant data to enhance accuracy; and (4) isolating individual failures through differential analysis. We showcase the efficacy of our approach by applying it to both real-world network traffic and simulated data, where it consistently outperforms more complex methods. Moreover, while some current methods may require significant computational resources, our approach has been specifically designed to function efficiently in resource-constrained environments. In terms of performance, we find that it surpasses others in terms of accuracy, while achieving a high true positive rate and incurring only a negligible increase in processing time. In fact, experiments have shown that the runtime of our approach is on average 30% faster than others. Furthermore, both the techniques and the associated code for change point detection without models, and the methods and code for change point detection with models, are freely accessible online. Specifically, they can be downloaded from the following locations: \href{https://github.com/jase-clarkson/adaptcp}{this GitHub repository} for the former, and \href{https://github.com/jase-clarkson/cpmt}{this GitHub repository} for the latter. Additionally, the refined failure isolation code can also be found at \href{https://github.com/jase-clarkson/ri}{this GitHub repository}. We encourage the broader research community to build upon and adapt our work for their own applications. \end{comment}

Acquiring large amounts of labeled data is a time-consuming, costly process for machine learning algorithms. Selective labeling techniques aim to mitigate this issue by assigning labels only to specific, difficult cases, leveraging model predictions as proxies for expert judgment. However, traditional methods struggle to accurately assess the model's performance on unlabelled data. In response, we introduce the Augmented Projected Gradient Descent (APGD) algorithm for assigning labels in an iterative manner. The APGD algorithm addresses three key challenges: generating high-quality pseudo-labels, adjusting labeling rates, and refining the model. Experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world data reveal that APGD outperforms existing methods under a range of conditions. Recent studies on model pruning have yielded substantial gains, yet the reduced models often exhibit a noticeable drop in performance. To address this limitation, researchers have developed techniques involving knowledge distillation to preserve model accuracy after pruning. Nonetheless, existing knowledge-based pruning methods are often hampered by issues such as incomplete knowledge transfer and the requirement for extensive training times. To overcome these challenges, we propose ClickTrain, a novel end-to-end knowledge-based pruning framework that accelerates pruning and optimizes model accuracy. ClickTrain leverages two key mechanisms: (1) it generates critical connection masks during training by incorporating an adversarial loss that enhances model robustness against pruning; and (2) it employs a novel pruning protocol that facilitates transfer of knowledge from large models to their compressed counterparts via multiple iterations of distillation and pruning. Experimental evaluations on ResNet, MobileNetV2, and SeNet models on ImageNet datasets demonstrate that ClickTrain achieves superior performance and faster convergence compared to previous knowledge-based pruning methods. Furthermore, ClickTrain offers substantial improvements over traditional pruning methods, yielding up to a 10% boost in performance with comparable compression rates. This allows us to derive natural completeness proofs for specific axioms within this framework, such as from the narrow norms for intuitionistic logic to the negative introduction sequents in the intuitionistic calculus. Additionally, we identify a dual completeness theorem for a wide range of substructural modal logics, including variants of classical and intuitionistic logic. The proposed relational semantics can be extended to accommodate additional substructural amenities. Furthermore, we show that every narrow norm on a relational model can be approximated by a sequence of elementary norms, facilitating a straightforward proof of the completeness of PTL. We also illustrate the application of relational semantics to norm-free substructural modal logics through the derivation of sound and complete axioms for such systems. We've developed a kNN classifier designed to recognize mathematical symbols within handwritten equations. This classifier leverages a unique feature space constructed by combining pixel intensity and frequency information from input images. Through experimentation with the ER2 dataset, we've identified that this classifier achieves exceptional accuracy, particularly in scenarios where data is scarce. Furthermore, we've successfully applied this approach to tackle the 'Math for Code' challenge, outperforming existing benchmarks. Additionally, we've devised two methods to enhance the classifier's performance: first, by using super-resolved images to boost performance; and second, by combining multiple kNN classifiers with varying feature space dimensions. These enhancements have yielded promising results in equation recognition. Notably, we've discovered that these methods can also be applied to text recognition tasks. Epidemic spreading in complex networks can be anticipated by examining certain characteristics. Researchers have made headways in forecasting epidemic outbreaks based on a network's overall structure. In this study, we test the validity of these predictions by examining a sophisticated network of college students in South Korea. To calculate the expectancy of an epidemic, we used two different methods: one grounded in mean-field theory and the other involving random graph modeling. Furthermore, we analyzed how network divisions and individual characteristics influence the spread of diseases. Notably, we discovered that two factors contribute to the predictability of an epidemic: the network's structure and the connectivity between groups. While our mean-field-based prediction showed promise, it fell short of the mark in this case study. In contrast, the random graph model yielded a more accurate prediction. This study provides valuable insights into using network structures to forecast epidemic spreading. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to utilize real-world student network data to make predictions about epidemic outbreaks. As a result, this research has significant implications for designing targeted mitigation strategies. Additionally, we propose an alternative approach that utilizes individual characteristics to improve epidemic predictions. To verify the robustness of our findings, we employed two techniques: altering the network structure and changing the epidemic parameters. Furthermore, we investigated the effects of group divisions on epidemic spreading in a network. To facilitate reproducibility, we have made the code and data used in this study available for public access. In conclusion, this study highlights the importance of considering both network structures and individual characteristics when forecasting and understanding epidemic spreading. This is especially pertinent in a world where global health crises and targeted interventions are increasingly important. Furthermore, this research highlights the potential for utilizing network analysis to make predictions about epidemic outbreaks in various settings. In future studies, we aim to explore the applications of machine learning algorithms in network analysis to make more accurate predictions about epidemic spreading. To achieve this, we plan to collect larger and more comprehensive datasets of network connections. In addition, we will investigate how individual behavior affects the spread of diseases in a network, with a focus on using this information to develop targeted mitigation strategies. This research has significant potential to make a positive impact in the world of public health by using network analysis to make accurate and action able predictions about epidemic outbreaks. In the long run, this research aims to contribute to the development of new methods for using network analysis to make predictions about complex systems that can be applied in a variety of domains. This is especially pertinent in a world where complex problems and global issues are increasingly important.

We propose an innovative technique to address the challenge of safety constraints in reinforcement learning. Unlike current methods that resolve safety breaches in real-time or anticipate them but sometimes miss actual violations, our technique allows for the incorporation of safety constraints into the reward function. By doing so, we ensure that agents are trained to respect these constraints while engaged in the learning process. Furthermore, our method leverages proximal policy optimization to facilitate efficient policy updates, enhancing the convergence rate. We validate the effectiveness of our technique by successfully training an agent to safely navigate a challenging obstacle course and simulating system failures, such as engine breakdowns, without violating safety constraints like maintaining vehicle stability. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves a higher convergence rate compared to existing techniques while achieving a higher success rate in completing tasks without safety breaches. We present the associated code on our GitHub repository: https://github.com/asharifi/proximal-safe-ppo. Additionally, we provide a detailed explanation of our method in a companion technical report (Arash Sharifi, 2020). The code has been updated to reflect any corrections to the original report. Moreover, we include the description of a variant of our method that uses Safe Action Embeddings (SafeAE) for generating action sequences that adhere to safety standards in reinforcement learning applications. By utilizing a classifier similar to that in the Expected Safety Features (ESF) method, our SafeAE technique creates a safe action sequence by embedding actions that comply with safety standards. We then utilize a transformer layer to generate a safe action sequence by sampling from the safety-constrained distribution of action embeddings. We validate the effectiveness of our SafeAE technique by successfully training an agent to complete tasks while adhering to safety standards in a reinforcement learning application. We have developed a novel control framework for mobile robots that utilizes a layered control system. This is particularly demonstrated through the integration of sonar sensors into a robot, enabling it to create a detailed map of its surroundings. Our approach is inspired by the Bayesian Filtering technique, incorporating both forward prediction and feedback correction to navigate effectively. As a result, the robot is able to efficiently create a precise geographical map and simultaneously localize itself within that space. We have achieved a notable improvement in navigation by utilizing this layered control framework, achieving accurate localization results even in environments as basic as a straight corridor. We have also compared our method to popular alternatives within the field of mobile robotics. In addition to the benefits mentioned, our layered control framework has several key advantages, including the ability to handle sensors that are not perfectly reliable and move on a plane that is not perfectly flat. We have successfully put this new framework to use in a navigation system for a mobile robot, and the results are presented in this paper. We have tested the framework using a simulated environment as well as two physical robots, one of which is equipped with 7 sonar sensors and the other with 12 sonar sensors. The results of these experiments have been detailed in this paper, and the findings indicate that our approach is able to achieve high levels of accuracy in a variety of situations while also being relatively easy to understand and implement. In a 2019 paper by Awanesov and Blass, it was introduced a way to utilize models of first-order set theory through the lens of Tukey-order. This concept enabled them to demonstrate several key implications between different cardinal characteristics. Notably, Awanesov and Blass showed that a certain combination of cardinal characteristics is interdependent, effectively rendering some of these characteristics interchangeable. This notion was further expanded upon in a 2020 paper by the current author and Tomkowicz, where it was applied to examine the Tukey-order of models of second-order arithmetic. This investigation sought to explore whether a similar interdependence exists among second-order arithmetic models. Although an absolute proof could not be found, it is shown that under certain syntactic constraints in second-order arithmetic, the Tukey-order does exhibit a strong interdependence structure. This result is significant and reveals that in a significant portion of the traditional subsystems of second-order arithmetic, the Tukey-order can be fully aligned with the standard ordering of cardinal characteristics. Furthermore, this work introduces a new method of analyzing Tukey-order for a broad class of mathematical theories, effectively providing a powerful tool for future use in theoretical computer science. Lastly, a key insight gained from this investigation could potentially offer a new approach for handling provability logic, by allowing for a possible alignment of the provability order with the standard ordering of cardinal characteristics. This idea could be particularly fruitful in certain specific contexts, such as in transfinite logic and other related theories. Conversely, it is also shown how certain properties unique to provability logic may prevent an absolute proof of the interdependence of the Tukey-order for first-order set theory. This realization highlights the importance of considering the distinct properties and limitations of different logical frameworks when applying the Tukey-order concept. Ultimately, this investigation contributes a significant advancement in the use of the Tukey-order concept, while also revealing promising avenues for future research in the field of mathematical logic. Additionally, an appendix is provided that contains an innovative application of the Tukey-order to examine the connection between infinitary consistency and provability in second-order arithmetic. This analysis sheds new light on an existing theory known as the bounded complement property and reveals a connection to consistency properties stemming from infinitary consistency, which in turn is linked to consistency properties of infinitary logic across multiple levels of infinitarity. Integrating the pessimism principle into bandit models enhances their robustness in complex situations. Building on this integration, we have developed a novel variant of Thompson sampling, termed pseudo-posterior Thompson sampling. This new approach is a constant-time, near-optimal learning strategy that is illogical to perpetuate suboptimal actions. We have also proven its asymptotic optimality and demonstrated its enhanced performance in dynamic treatment regimes when compared to the current state-of-the-art method. Furthermore, our research has established a near-optimal constant-time learning framework and provided a constructive approach to extend this framework to pseudo-posterior learning. We used the framework to develop a near-optimal constant-time dynamic treatment policy, offering a significant improvement over the existing optimal policy in scenarios with limited observations. We further supplemented our findings with a set of simulation-based examples showcasing its enhanced practical outcomes. We have made the associated code publicly available on the GitHub platform (https://github.com/alim117/Hierarchical_Pseudo-Posterior_Thompson_Sampling). In this study, we explore  p-adic solenoids with a metric derived from p-adic norms. By employing the metric, we define the space of continuous functions from this solenoid to another p-adic solenoid and establish a functional equation for an analog of the Legendre symbol. We demonstrate that this analog shares a key similarity with the Jacobi symbol. Furthermore, a case of the Fourier transform for functions defined on a p-adic circle group is examined, and solutions to this problem are presented for specific scenarios involving ultra-metrical functions and functions with restricted growth. We also extend the Polya theorem to the context of p-adic solenoids, and present novel results concerning the representation of integer-valued functions on p-adic circles. 

In addition to these main findings, supplementary studies are presented on the representation of functions taking values in a limited set of integers and on the classification of groups with a p-adic structure. These results share some connections with the works of E. Artin, B. Huppert, S. Lefschetz, N. Koblitz and D. Gondodipuro. 

The study presented here is a p-adic analogue of a corresponding study in the framework of real numbers, published under the title 'Continuous functions with restricted growth and the generalized Polya theorem', by A. A. Bostrom, H. P. Cohen and D. Shanks.

To evaluate the effectiveness of different clustering algorithms on presence-absence data, we conducted an in-depth comparison of eight popular methods. These methods include Autoencoders, k-means, hierarchical clustering with Ward's or Euclidean distance, OPTICS, DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, OPTICSTree, and PCARE. To assess their performance, we utilized a comprehensive set of 108 real-life and synthetic datasets across various dimensions, spanning from 20 to 5,000 species. Datasets were categorized into three types: randomly generated, pseudo-realistic, and based on actual species data from the Island Biogeography and Bird Species scenarios. Our analysis covered aspects such as clustering purity, the number of clusters it detected, and the computational time required. Ultimately, we determined that k-means produced the most consistent and accurate results across all datasets, while hierarchical clustering with Euclidean distance was a close second. However, these traditional methods struggled with higher dimensional datasets, revealing that more advanced algorithms like HDBSCAN and DBSCAN were more effective in such situations, producing better purity scores. Nonetheless, they often overestimated the number of clusters. Based on our findings, we recommended k-means for general use in presence-absence data analysis due to its balanced performance in terms of accuracy, cluster identification, and computational efficiency. While hierarchical clustering was suitable for smaller datasets, our results suggested that more than 50 species presented challenges to its effectiveness. Conversely, the more sophisticated clustering algorithms may be more suitable for specific research needs, such as large-scale species data analysis or the detection of presences and absences in presence-absence data up to 5,000 species. Ultimately, the choice of algorithm should be informed by the specific research objectives, data characteristics, and the desired outcomes. To facilitate this process, we have made our code and dataset available for public use. Additionally, a set of 292 bird species from the Bird Species scenario has been uploaded to the open access repository Zenodo for the benefit of the scientific community. Developing effective machine learning algorithms for tasks that require extensive training data can be challenging, particularly when the training samples are limited. The creation of realistic samples of handwritten text is such a problem - generating high-quality, realistic handwriting samples from minimal data is an extremely difficult task. Researchers previously proposed Bayesian Program Learning (BPL) and demonstrated its potential in creating human-like handwriting samples with minimal training data, but its effectiveness in text generation was limited to short strings. This study aimed to expand BPL capabilities to complex text generation while maintaining its ability to generalize with minimal training data. We achieved this by incorporating BPL with a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) and tested its effectiveness in generating handwritten text. The results of our study confirmed the expected outcomes - the integration of BPL with VAE significantly improved the quality of generated text samples, as well as the algorithm's ability to generalize to new text patterns with minimal training data. We also observed that the program learning component tended to dominate the text generation process, resulting in a more efficient use of minimal training data. Ultimately, the integrated model produced high-quality text samples that closely matched the quality of those generated using BPL, despite being rendered unreadable due to the excessive randomness introduced by VAE. This research has significant implications for the development of more effective machine learning algorithms that can generate realistic samples from minimal data, particularly in applications where the training samples are limited. We present the results of our study as a potential solution to the challenges of sample efficient learning, particularly in the domain of handwritten text generation. By combining a hierarchical block-based approach with a tree-like memory pool structure, DynaSOAr has successfully minimized fragmentation, optimized allocation speed, and maximized scalability. The experimental results show that DynaSOAr achieves substantial performance gains, including a 78$\times$ speedup, and greatly reduces fragmentation by 99.9%, compared to traditional allocators. Furthermore, DynaSOAr has the unique capability of providing accurate real-time memory usage statistics for complex GPU workloads. In addition, DynaSOAr has the potential to inspire new algorithmic innovations for GPU programming. In the future, DynaSOAr may be used to support memory-intensive GPU applications in various fields such as medicine, video surveillance, astrophysics, and weather forecasting. To illustrate the value of this metric, which can inform hypothesis testing and optimal decision rules, we consider two key cases: (1) simple, binary decision functions and abundant data, and (2) complex decision functions and limited data. In the first instance, we demonstrate that robustness can be efficiently calculated via Monte Carlo simulation and provide a straightforward method for approximating its value. In the second case, we suggest a simulation-based approximation of the robustness metric. Notably, both of these methods are general-purpose tools that can be applied across a wide range of situations. The creation of a supersolid state in a Bose-Einstein condensate is commonly studied using theoretical models that investigate how weak impurities within the system affect its strong interactions, essentially acting as a 'perturbator'. In the past, research has primarily focused on the system's static properties, utilizing complex mathematical techniques such as diagrammatic approaches and variational methods to analyze the impact of the impurity's movement on the system's properties. In a groundbreaking approach, our study uses advanced computer simulation to investigate the dynamic behavior of a supersolid system with an oscillating impurity, revealing its influence on phonon modes and the system's roton minimum. This theory allows for a flexible decomposition of optimization problems into a set of smoother sub-problems that can be solved independently and simultaneously to create a sequence of potential solutions. These solutions are then merged into a optimal solution using the minimum descent path strategy. Performance advantages are observed in terms of faster computational time and higher success rates of convergence to a local optimum. Experimental analysis also reveals that the complexity of convergence converges to O(N^2), where N represents the number of total pixels in an image sequence. Future research could investigate how the proposed algorithm could be applied to other optimization challenges, such as medical image segmentation, object detection, and video analysis. A statistical analysis of magnetic bright points was conducted, focusing on their occurrence, distribution, velocity, and energy across the solar surface. The chosen data came from the SDO's high-speed imaging system, specifically the 430 nm wavelength, and covered a period of nearly two years. The findings indicated that MBPs occur more frequently near solar active regions and are more common during periods of increased activity. The PPT square conjecture suggests that a pseudo-entanglement, when transformed into its dual form, remains entangled. Initially, this hypothesis was supported by computational evidence in finite-dimensional spaces. This paper goes a step further by establishing a method to construct PPT pseudo-entanglements in dimension $d \times d$, where $d$ represents a positive integer, and demonstrates that these can be distinct from their tensor product equivalents. Additionally, we present graphic representations of PPT pseudo-entanglements in dimension $5 \times 5$ and $6 \times 6$. Notably, we show that PPT pseudo-entanglements can be found within locally invertible matrices. This finding has significant implications as it implies that locally invertible matrices cannot be expressed as positive semi-definite matrices. This contrasts with Lagrangian Grassmannians, where such a decomposition is possible. Furthermore, we propose the idea of entanglement lines, where the connection between locally invertible matrices and the PPT square conjecture may hold the key to understanding entanglement structure in affine spaces. Lastly, we explore the application of qubit-qubit bipartite PPT pseudo-entanglements in the generation of locally invertible cloners, a device used in quantum information theory to assess the stability of cloners based on their entanglement structure. The unique transport mechanisms in neurons are integral to various cellular processes, including axonal transport of materials necessary for neuronal function and integrity. The intricate internal structures of neurons, which consist of microtubules, neuronal filaments, and transport vesicles, are still not fully understood, particularly how materials are transferred between them. A new study utilizes data-driven methods to investigate how the geometric properties of microtubules, enforced by dynamic assembly and disassembly, affect transport patterns. The research reveals that transport along microtubules is efficient when they adopt a straight conformation, but becomes obstructed when they curl. Additionally, the findings indicate that transport vesicles are drawn towards growing ends of microtubles, which undergo dynamic assembly. The results are consistent with axonal transport patterns observed in neurons and suggest a role for microtubule geometry in facilitating transport across long distances. Furthermore, the study's outcomes could be applied to understanding the transport of materials in other cell types. The research was conducted by a collaborative effort between the Velasco-Hidalgo, Schaefer, and Lindenberg groups at Princeton University's Department of Chemistry and the Center for Molecular Biotechnology. The research was supported by the National Science Foundation, the Princeton Center for Computational Innovation, and Princeton's High Performance Computing Facility. The researchers express their gratitude to these institutions for their support. A peer-reviewed article detailing the research has been published in the journal Cell Reports Physical Science under the title "Microtubule dynamics and geometry influence transport patterns" [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xplscr.2021.100699]. A video summarizing the research is available on YouTube at https://youtu.be/6Y7QeQqQqEg. KTH, 2021.

When a non-rotating white dwarf in a binary system exceeds the critical mass of 1.38 solar masses and reaches the point of collapse into a black or neutron star, mass loss from the white dwarf forms an accretion disc surrounding the new compact object. For binary systems containing a white dwarf and a main sequence star with a mass greater than approximately 0.4 solar masses, the process of mass loss from the white dwarf typically results in the formation of an accretion disc. However, direct observations of accretion discs surrounding black holes or neutron stars in binary systems containing a main sequence star and a white dwarf are rare, with one notable exception involving the binary system Cyg X-4. Although the white dwarf in Cyg X-4 has a mass of 3 solar masses, which is significantly greater than the critical value of 1.38 solar masses, mass loss from the white dwarf does not form an accretion disc surrounding the black hole or neutron star components. Instead, mass loss from the binary system as a whole is thought to be responsible for the observed accretion disc. In an effort to understand this phenomenon, we conducted a series of three-dimensional simulations of the binary system Cyg X-4. Our results indicate that during close approaches of the two stars, the neutron star accretion rate becomes saturated at a maximum value due to the efficient blocking of the inflowing material by the neutron star's disc, with mass loss from the white dwarf resulting in mass jets rather than an accretion disc surrounding the black hole or neutron star components. Our findings also show that mass loss from the binary system as a whole may be responsible for the observed accretion disc surrounding the neutron star component in Cyg X-4. Additionally, our model is consistent with the observed light curves of the binary system Cyg X-4 during various orbital phases. Our experimental design, coupled with our subsequent data analysis, indicates that mass loss from the white dwarf forms a disc around the compact object only when the compact object is a black hole resulting from a supernova explosion, rather than through the transfer of material from the main sequence star. This paper delves into the concept of rootings within branchings of complete graphs, particularly in examining minors. It has been demonstrated that for any given root of a complete graph on t vertices, a specific branch set containing all possible t-element subsets except one can be identified as a minor. Furthermore, it was discovered that certain root branchings containing all t-element subsets are minors in certain classes of monotone hypergraphs. In addition, upper limits to the number of roots in t-chromatic graphs without specific branch minors have been established. These findings contribute to the resolution of prior conjectures and expand upon existing research in this field. In fact, the results presented here can be seen as a culmination of efforts to address a central problem (Problem 1 in [10]) regarding root branchings and chromatic hypergraphs. We investigate a network of superconducting qubits functioning as universal quantum interfaces, capable of forming long-distance connected qubits through 'entangling collision' triggers. By adjusting the trigger method, we optimize quantum states and observe significant increases in Fisher information, ultimately reaching nearly optimal levels. The performance depends on the trigger strategy and can be enhanced further by refining the qubit design, utilizing quantum feedback, and implementing more sophisticated state preparations. The novel concept of entangling collisions in quantum optics enables the development of highly sensitive quantum networks, paving the way for breakthroughs in quantum metrology and information science.

We establish new bounds for the first eigenvalue of the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator subject to a second-type Robin boundary condition. Dependence on the parameter $\beta$ and parameters $q$ and $p$ is considered. Furthermore, we find sharp bounds expressed in terms of norm and a factor involving $\gamma(p,q)$, a measure of anisotropy. Investigation of the influence of parameter $\beta$ yields results expressed in terms of $\min\{p,q\}$. Notably, when $p$ equals $q$, we derive expressions for eigenvalue bounds that are expressed in terms of $\sin(\pi\beta)/\cos(\pi\beta)$. In addition to these theoretical findings, we provide examples that verify the validity of our bounds and demonstrate their sharpness. We examine an explicit model problem with a non-standard boundary condition and another with a boundary condition featuring both second- and first-type components. Both of these model studies showcase that boundary condition type influences eigenvalue behavior and can be studied using variation methods. Moreover, we investigate an alternative approach to Robin problems using trace operators in Hilbert spaces, illustrating its applicability and usefulness to problem variants with parameter dependence. Ultimately, we conclude that this approach may be applicable to investigating bounds on problems involving fractional Laplacian and Robin boundary conditions. Our conclusions are codified in two statements. Moreover, the related work on Robin problems highlights its inherent intricacies and instabilities, compounded by anisotropy, which may preclude obtaining second-type Robin eigenvalue spectra using variational methods. Consequently, we suggest that third-type Robin problems, which are known to be variational but unstable, may offer insight into physical phenomena. Consequently, we propose that anisotropic third-type Robin problems may provide necessary and sufficient conditions for problem solvability, which could expand the set of solvable problems. Recent studies link Graph Convolutional Networks to conventional Convolutional Neural Networks and fully connected Neural Networks via the Graph Convolution operator. However, implementing this operator is challenging due to the need for inverse graph Laplacian approximation. In this research, we connect this operator to the Graph Fourier Transform, similar to how the Inverse Fourier Transform recovers an image from its frequency domain representation. To prove this connection, we propose two proofs, one of which assumes the Network's layers are infinitely thick. We also establish that the Graph Fourier Transform can be implemented using the Graph Laplacian's inverse, but with the added benefit of avoiding the approximation issue. This finding suggests a novel, differentiable Graph Fourier Transform module that can be used within Graph Convolutional Networks to achieve exact results. In addition to this module, we propose a new module based on the Graph Laplacian's inverse that can aid in feature extraction from connected graph data. Both modules outperform current methods in various regression and graph classification tasks. In particular, our Graph Fourier Transform module achieves better results on tasks involving connected graph data in comparison to existing Graph Convolutional Networks. Furthermore, the combination of the Graph Fourier Transform module and the inverse module yields state-of-the-art results on the GraphNN and Prokion benchmarks in graph classification tasks. The project addresses the issue of data scarcity in Parsing Guidelines by creating a self-training technique that incorporates deep contextual information. Unlike traditional self-training, which relies on gold annotations to enhance model performance, our deep contextualized self-training (DCST) algorithm makes use of neural network bi-directional contextual representations. These representations, obtained from a pre-trained bi-directional LSTM model, are used to improve model performance through self-training. Our experiments were conducted on 30 languages across various datasets, including Treebanks, Universal Parsebank, and those associated with languages such as Russian, Hebrew, Arabic and Chinese. The results show that DCST achieves significant gains over current best practices in parsing, while also paving the way for future advancements in Natural Language Processing. Our findings indicate that with sufficient parallel data, the performance of parsing can approach levels similar to those of sentence classification, both in terms of accuracy and F1 measure. Furthermore, our analysis of the role of gold annotations in parsing suggests that there may be future cost savings through semi-supervised or self-training methods aimed at reducing the need for extensive annotation. We propose a method for discovering the fusion tables of non-trivial, invertible symmetries for any quantum field theory that has a well-defined algebra of symmetries. This method also applies to both local and non-local cases. Furthermore, we suggest a way to determine the fusion rules for non-invertible symmetries, which is achievable if we can identify and manipulate the braiding and composition of any two operators whose algebra is known. This method is illustrated using simple examples of quantum critical and quantum insulating models. Additionally, we demonstrate how to calculate the central charge of a quantum critical system using the fusion spectrum of its non-trivial symmetries, which includes both local and non-local cases. Finally, we examine how to construct new models of quantum critical and insulating systems using any given quantum critical system, based on known modular invariant partitions of the fusion table of one of its non-trivial, invertible symmetry generators. This model-building approach is most relevant and useful for 2D quantum systems, but it may also be extended to 3D systems with global symmetries. Specifically, we use the Ising model and the $\mathbb Z_2$ toric code as examples of this quantum model-building technique. Furthermore, we discuss how to use the fusion table of any given quantum insulating system to create new quantum insulating systems, which is a 2D equivalent of the Kitaev model's construction in 2D. Lastly, we discuss future research prospects based on our method's limitations. Some of these potential future research prospects include using our method in the study of systems with local conformal symmetry, using our method in the study of systems with global symmetry but no local conformal symmetry, and using our method in the study of systems with global symmetry and non-invertible exotic symmetry generators. Additionally, we potentially discuss the use of our method in the study of systems with global symmetry and non-invertible quantum dualality symmetry generators. Conversely, we also discuss systems in which our method does not currently apply, such as systems with global symmetry and non-invertible braiding symmetry generators, systems in which the braiding algebra is unknown, and systems in which the composition algebra is unknown. Lastly, we potentially discuss the use of our method in the study of systems with global symmetry and non-invertible quantum twist dualty symmetry generators. We investigate the complexity of categorically definable sets in unary countable structures, particularly those based on finite fields. Considering the field of ratios from a finite set of primes, we examine linear systems of equations with coefficients from this field. It's found that the existence of solutions for such systems, regardless of order, isn't categorically definable within unary countable structures. On the other hand, we can determine the categoricity of some specific systems, like those with unique solutions for every equation. This leads us to explore specific properties of finite fields and their prime fields, as well as to establish a categorization theorem for unary countable structures based on their behavior with field operations and relation to prime fields. This application allows us to pinpoint categorically definable sets within specific unary countable structures, such as those involving rational fields and fields of p-adic numbers. Moreover, we show that every unary countable structure has an expansion to a rigid structure, which can be categorized based on its invariant theory. This expansion allows for the preservation of the first-order theory and eliminates any non-rigid behavior within unary countable structures. Additionally, we use this result to establish a categorization theorem for unary countable structures with limit-type operators, which encompasses various types of limit behaviors including those for rational and p-adic limits. Finally, we show that every unary countable structure has an expansion to a structure with a categorical rigid chain, which can be chosen to maintain a first-order theory equivalence. This allows for the preservation of the first-order theory and eliminates any non-rigid behavior within unary countable structures. Moreover, we use this result to establish a categorization theorem for unary countable structures with order isomorphisms to a chain, which encompasses various types of order behaviors including those for rational and p-adic orders. Also, we show that the class of linear systems with coefficients from a finite field is not categorically definable in unary countable structures, which can be seen as an extension of a previous result for finite prime fields as stated in our companion paper. Instead, we can determine the categoricity of some specific systems, like those with unique solutions for every equation. This leads us to explore specific properties of finite fields and their prime fields, as well as to establish a categorization theorem for unary countable structures based on their behavior with field operations and relation to prime fields. This application allows us to pinpoint categorically definable sets within specific unary countable structures, such as those involving rational fields and fields of p-adic numbers.

We have performed an in-depth investigation of the electronic and magnetic properties of the doped series (Eu$_{1-x}$Bi$_{x}$)2Ir2O7 within the tunable electron-doped Eu2Ir2O7 system. Through a combination of experimental techniques including x-ray photoemission spectroscopy, x-ray absorption spectroscopy, and magnetization measurements, along with detailed calculations utilizing the cluster perturbation theory method within the dynamical mean-field approach, our results reveal the distinct impact of electron doping using Bi$^{3+}$ on the unique $6s$ electronic state of bismuth. By systematically increasing the Bi doping fraction ($x$$\leq$$0.20$), we observe substantial changes in the spectral intensity at approximately $0.5$ eV within the valence band, along with shifts in energy and increased spin-orbit coupling within the final state of the Bi $6s$ photoelectron. However, these effects are confined to the $6s$ state, and our data indicate that Bi doping has a relatively minor influence on the underlying electronic and magnetic properties of the Eu2Ir2O7 compound. Despite this, our study does suggest the presence of Bi$^{1+}$ ions, alongside an ordered lattice of Eu$^{2+}$ ions and an iridate block that remains close to a Mott insulating state. Our findings also suggest that further increasing the Bi doping fraction may lead to the stabilization of various magnetic phases, along with a spin glass phenomenon that emerges at higher Bi doping levels ($x$$\geq$$0.15$). Ultimately, our research presents a comprehensive understanding of the electronic, magnetic, and phase evolutionary behavior within the (Eu$_{1-x}$Bi$_{x}$)2Ir2O7 doped series. Based on these results, we anticipate the discovery of novel magnetic phases and potentially new quantum phenomena within similar electron-doped 5$d$ transition metal oxides.

We derive strict limitations on the magnitude of the worst-case rankings for n-tuples with dimensions n ≥ 5, establishing that in such cases, the relative ranking of the items must be approximately linear. Additionally, our findings refine and consolidate previous research on the classification of nontransitive n-tuples. We also develop a method for categorizing negative n-tuples as transitive or nontransitive and establish a time complexity bound of O(n^2 log n). The proliferation of software variants and configurations through options
such as enable/disable has led to a significant buildup of options that are
not actively utilized within the software's source code. This undesired growth
not only hampers the software's maintainability but also renders compilation
processes longer and more cumbersome. In the realm of product configuration,
research has focused on removing unneeded features; however, little attention has
been devoted to exploring an analogous approach for software's run-time
configuration. This study aims to address an unresolved question: can system
administrators and developers benefit from stripping away unused run-time options?
To answer this, we introduce an novel approach known as RTUnOptions, which
automates the process of disabling unused run-time options. Employing the Linux
kernel as our target platform, we show that RTUnOptions is effective in
identifying and disabling uncustomized options, demonstrating a significant
reduction of 35% in options with minimal negative impact on system performance. 
This reduction in options ekes out minor gains in system processing speed and
saves memory, albeit marginal, with performance differences observable only at
extreme scales. Nonetheless, these findings underscore the value of
retrospective maintenance activities, such as decoupling and removing unused
components, in enhancing the software's configuration layer. Furthermore, these
results hint at further potential optimizations for system performance by
restricing the scope of run-time options. Lastly, the Open-source research project

A novel method for dark matter detection is introduced in this paper, focusing on the measurable impact of dark matter-nucleus interactions on ionization processes within solid dark matter detection materials. The ionization effect can be significant, particularly when supplemented by free electrons generated from nuclear interactions. We detail the key factors influencing this phenomenon and develop an simulation tool to calculate the associated ionization yields, which are essential for setting detection limits in future experiments. By incorporating these yields into the standard analysis of dark matter-induced nuclear recoils, experimental limits can be tightened. As an example, our analysis shows that ionization constraints can significantly impact the detection of inelastic scattering events involving dark matter and solid materials. More broadly, this method can be applied to a broader range of DM models that shift the detection limit into the more favorable parameter space. Additionally, the methodology presented can be applied to the analysis of data collected during past as well as upcoming experimental runs.
