ECG signal analysis is fundamental in cardiovascular disease diagnosis and has been extensively studied for extracting inter-beat intervals and heart rate variability information that pose significant challenges, especially with noisy signals. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning technology have shown the potential to significantly improve the extraction of IBI from ECG signals, offering improved accuracy and robustness over traditional methods. In this study, we present a deep learning-based method that utilizes data-driven and model-driven parallel training to enhance the extraction of IBI from noisy ECG signals. By combining normalizing transformations and feature extraction layers, along with data augmentation techniques, we achieved highly accurate results of 97.4% for normal beats, 94.6% for ventricular ectopic beats, 96.2% for fusion beats, and 98.2% for supraventricular ectopic beats. Furthermore, the method exhibited exceptional performance in noise-resistant ECG signal estimation, demonstrating enhanced robustness and accuracy compared to traditional approaches. Notably, the method also demonstrated promising results in distinguishing different types of heart rhythms and predicting subsequent RR intervals. We anticipate that this method will contribute to the development of advanced diagnostic and predictive techniques for heart disease using ECG signals. The distinction between harmonic and anharmonic potentials is scrutinized in the context of active force generation. Investigating a one-dimensional system with a fluctuating external force and a particle undergoing periodic back-and-forth movements, researchers discovered notable variations in how fluctuations behave compared to thermal equilibrium conditions. Specifically, in the case of anharmonic potentials, fluctuations exhibit enhanced activity while showing a decline in power law behavior as the frequency approaches the maximum. In contrast, harmonic potentials display distinct, non-power law behavior at peak frequencies. Notably, these findings align with recent research on active force generation and also mirror the analysis of legitimate active force experiments, where differences in active behavior between anharmonic and harmonic potentials are evident. We therefore propose the use of these findings as a means of validating active force experiments. We also demonstrate that the fluctuations observed in the experiments can be utilized to determine the coefficient of the anharmonic potential, thus providing a reliable method for extracting accurate information from the experiments. We further extend our analysis to multi-dimensional systems, where the distinction between harmonic and anharmonic potentials becomes particularly relevant, and where the active fluctuations exhibit intriguing characteristics, particularly in the absence of external forces. The detailed modeling of human faces is a complex task due to the intricate anatomy of the face and the diverse range of expressions that need to be accurately captured. Existing methods are limited in their ability to create a richly detailed 3D model of a human expression. In response, we introduce HUMBI, an approach that uses a multi-scale representation of expression transitions to create a more photorealistic 3D model of a human expression. By analyzing the spatial relationships between different facial features, HUMBI can identify the key features that are most important for creating a detailed 3D model of a human expression. In addition, HUMBI can use temporal information to refine the 3D model of an expression. In our experiments, we demonstrate that HUMBI can produce a more detailed 3D model of an expression that is similar to that of a human face. In particular, HUMBI outperformed the baseline method in creating a detailed 3D model of a human expression, with improvements of 13.6% and 3.8% in the FID and FVM metrics, respectively. Furthermore, HUMBI can use an iterative process to further improve the detailedness of the 3D model. In our experiments, we found that using multiple iterations of HUMBI led to continued improvements in the detailedness of the 3D model. With four iterations, HUMBI outperformed the baseline method in creating a detailed 3D model of a human expression, with improvements of 20.9% and 6.1% in the FID and FVM metrics, respectively. In terms of computational efficiency, HUMBI has a computational cost that is similar to that of the baseline method. In particular, both HUMBI and the baseline method take on the order of milliseconds to create a detailed 3D model of a human expression. In terms of the number of iterations, HUMBI has a computational cost that is linear, with a total computational cost of $O(n)$ where $n$ is the number of iterations. In particular, with four iterations, HUMBI has a total computational cost of $O(4)=4$. In terms of the method complexity, HUMBI has a complexity of $O(m)$ where $m$ is the number of complex components in the expression, with a total complexity of $O(m)$ to create a detailed 3D model of a human expression. In the field of optical character recognition (OCR), top-tier models have achieved exceptional performance, exceeding 90% accuracy in post-processing. Nonetheless, these models were initially developed and refined solely for use in a single language - English. To break linguistic barriers and make OCR more inclusive globally, a new multi-lingual model must be created. To accomplish this, we propose a groundbreaking model called M-DeViSE, an innovative solution for multi-lingual OCR. By integrating a novel, language-agnostic feature extraction module and a dynamic, language-switching decoder module, M-DeViSE can accurately recognize and adapt to various writing systems without prior knowledge. Furthermore, M-DeViSE can handle a vast number of languages simultaneously, overcoming the limitations of existing models that require extensive labeling for each new language. To validate the model's effectiveness, we conducted thorough evaluations on six languages, comparing M-DeViSE to leading models and achieving remarkable results, surpassing the current state-of-the-art by a significant margin. Notably, M-DeViSE can process images and translate them into text in real-time, demonstrating its potential for seamless integration into modern AI-assisted interfaces. You can explore M-DeViSE in action at https://mdevise-carrot.github.io/M-DeViSE/index.html. The model's source code is available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/Carrot/M-DeViSE. The model can be downloaded from https://huggingface.com/datasets/carrot/MDeViSE to replicate our results. Additionally, M-DeViSE can be installed as an Hugging Face transformer model using the command `huggingface hub fetch MDeViSE --no-validation` and then linked with the command `huggingface model link MDeViSE <hub_id>` after downloading the model from the Hub. Once the model is installed, it can be used for text recognition by running the command `huggingface interacton run MDeViSE --input_image <image_path>` to receive the decoded text output from the model. You can also modify the model's behavior by adding custom decoding strategies to the command `huggingface interacton run MDeViSE --decode_strategy <custom_strategy> --input_image <image_path>`. For a comprehensive list of available commands and usage examples, please refer to the model's official documentation at https://mdevise-carrot.github.io/M-DeViSE/docs/index.html. In video prediction, especially for video restoration tasks like video denoising, BasicVSR has established a new benchmark with impressive results. However, its performance could be further enhanced for lower frame rates like 30fps. The key limitations of BasicVSR are its weighted linear prediction methods, which lack adequate feature representation for video restoration at 30fps. The other issue is the complexity and memory requirements of its unweighted counterparts, making them impractical for such a frame rate. The proposed model, BasicVSR++, addresses these limitations through significant improvements. BasicVSR++ uses a novel linear dynamic network to replace traditional linear predictors for a more accurate feature representation. The model also leverages a temporal convolutional network as a prior for denoising, available for the first time at 30fps. The proposed architecture achieves state-of-the-art results on the denoising task while being more efficient than BasicVSR in terms of computational complexity and memory requirements. As a result, BasicVSR++ provides a 24% gain in PSNR and a 10% gain in model parameters over the baseline approach, with an comparable accuracy for higher frame rates. The proposed framework also opens doors for possible applications in video forecasting by reaching high accuracy levels at 30fps. The model's efficiency enables it to perform tasks like video inpainting and video deblurring with high quality, showcasing its potential in various video processing tasks. We investigate how a single dynamics model can be trained alongside two independent reinforcement learning agents, striving to control two distinct tasks. Our research reveals that a dynamics model trained in this manner becomes biased towards the first executed task. To mitigate this bias, we propose two new methods. Firstly, we've developed a way to train a dynamics model in a multi-task context while maintaining its neutrality. Secondly, we've devised an approach to correct any task-contamination that occurs during dynamics model training. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of both solutions in eliminating bias when using a shared dynamics model for multiple tasks. Furthermore, when the dynamics model is neutral, we show that it enables a second task to be learned up to 300% faster by the reinforcement learning agent. As for the task-correction method, we observed a dynamics model update rate reduction of as much as 60% while maintaining equivalent performance. These outcomes strongly suggest that a neutral dynamics model and task-correction techniques can effectively address bias-related issues when using a single dynamics model to accomplish multiple reinforcement learning tasks. Hurricanes that make landfall in areas like Florida can cause catastrophic damage to the power grid, leading to prolonged outages. To anticipate and mitigate these disruptions, utility companies and grid operators need to understand how hurricanes affect their service areas. By utilizing historical hurricane data and simulating weather conditions, such as high winds and rainfall, researchers can evaluate the impact of these storms on the power grid. This allows for identifying vulnerable transmission lines and assessing the extent of outages, which can inform preparedness and response efforts. To develop an advanced outage model, NASA's Ames Research Center partnered with the Electric Power Grid Research Center, leveraging their respective expertise in hurricane simulations and power systems. This collaboration resulted in the creation of a groundbreaking outage model, enabled by a high-performance computing platform, that simulates 3,600 hours of weather conditions, resulting in approximately 37,000 transmission line failures. This model can be scaled up to accommodate various weather scenarios, providing accurate forecasts to guide damage assessment and response in the event of a landfalling hurricane. To implement this outage model, researchers employed innovative solutions, such as data parallel processing, to optimize performance, and developed an open-source protocol to facilitate communication between weather and power systems simulations. This approach can be adapted for utility companies, grid operators, and researchers to assess and mitigate the effects of severe weather on the power grid. Furthermore, this work lays the foundation for incorporating real-time weather data into the outage model, enabling timely and accurate assessments. To achieve this, further developments in meteorological and power systems modeling are required, along with integration of actual power grid data, which could yield even more precise outcomes. To facilitate this advanced outage model, additional investments in high-performance computing infrastructure and expertise would be beneficial. To conclude, this collaboration successfully bridged the gap between hurricane and power grid simulations using high-performance computing, yielding a practical outage model that can inform landfalling hurricane response efforts. This partnership also fostered new research opportunities in both hurricane and power grid modeling, along with outreach efforts to utility companies, grid operators, and the wider research community. We define two classes of piecewise affine maps: those with natural encoding spaces limited by a finite bound, and those whose coding spaces match a specified subset. For the first class, we demonstrate that the map's coding space forms a subgroup of the original space, and for the second class, we prove the mapping is in fact a homomorphism. Ultimately, we establish that the second class includes all maps whose coding spaces align with the Dyck system, and this result holds even when using weaker conditions on the maps' images. Additionally, we provide a criterion for identifying if a piecewise isometry is in fact affine. Using this, we show examples of piecewise isometries with limited and infinite coding spaces. Lastly, we study the properties of maps whose coding spaces include only nilpotent words. In the process, we also address questions regarding the nilpotency of these maps' images. We provide numerical examples illustrating the maps' behavior. Furthermore, we establish that any nilpotent group can be represented as the image of a piecewise affine map whose coding space consists of nilpotent words. We also show examples of non-affine and non-isometric maps whose coding spaces consist of nilpotent words. It utilizes a cascaded network architecture to divide the spectral range into distinct segments, each captured by a DCT-based magnitude-only CNN. Temporal dependencies within each segment are explored using a DNN trained with TTS data. Unlike existing approaches, this model can effectively capture both spectral and temporal characteristics of speech without requiring a probabilistic framework. Experimental results demonstrate that CTS-MDCT achieves superior performance compared to the conventional TTS pipeline, specifically in terms of a lower PER for short-term errors and a lower OR for long-term errors. It also exhibits enhanced robustness against various signal manipulation techniques. Furthermore, the model shows great potential in generating realistic, long-lasting quasi-periodic signals. Given its versatility, CTS-MDCT is anticipated to be a crucial component in future neural TTS systems. Existing CF methods that utilize biclustering have excelled in addressing data scarcity and feature redundancy, yet they have overlooked the importance of user and item performance in the two dimensions. To address this limitation, a new approach called USBFC has been proposed, which applies unsupervised boundary finding on user and item performance to identify a unified similarity matrix. By incorporating boundary clustering, USBFC mitigates the over-fitting caused by binary partitioning and enables a more refined model. Experimental results demonstrate that USBFC surpasses the performance of conventional CF and deep CF methods on three datasets by a significant margin. Notably, USBFC has achieved top-notch performance compared to 26 recently-proposed CF methods on the Movielens-100K dataset. Furthermore, USBFC has successfully addressed data scarcity and feature redundancy in the datasets. The proposed model, USBFC, is now available for public use at the provided link.

The surface magnetic field of active stars plays a crucial role in understanding their activity levels, which are often evaluated using certain spectral lines as an indicator. However, these lines may not always accurately reflect the level of magnetic activity, especially in rapidly rotating stars. We examined the surface magnetic field of a sample of 26 active stars, primarily identified through the detection of H-alpha emission, and compared the results to existing studies. Our findings support the use of several other spectral indicators of magnetic activity, in addition to the traditional one, as they are less susceptible to biases caused by stellar rotation. Additionally, we found a significant correlation between the activity levels of these indicators and the stellar age, as well as a notable difference in activity levels between fast and slow rotators. We also found that the activity levels of the fastest rotators were generally lower than what was previously observed. Furthermore, we found no evidence of a relationship between the activity levels and the stellar mass, as might be expected. We discuss the implications of these findings for future studies of stellar activity and provide a list of stars that are candidates for having significant X-ray emission. We also made available a new code that can automatically measure the strengths of certain spectral indicators of magnetic activity from spectral observations, including both synthetic and real spectra. A novel experimental approach using high-speed imaging and image processing has been developed to study the settling behavior of snow crystals in a turbulent air stream. This setup enables the precise measurement of individual crystal trajectories over extended periods. The analysis focuses on a crystal's response to air currents and their interaction with larger snow aggregates. The results show that snow crystals' settling behavior can be categorized into three distinct velocity ranges, determined by their mass-to-dynamic-viscosity ratio (similar to the aerosol particle settling velocities in liquid media). For larger snow crystals within these velocity ranges, hydrodynamic effects are considered, and a model incorporating these effects is developed to align with experimental findings. The findings also reveal that at high Stokes numbers, crystals settle in a straight line, and, unlike aerosols, their settling velocity does not decline with increasing air stream velocities. Furthermore, the results show that the process of snow crystal aggregation within a given velocity range does not alter their settling behavior, and, importantly, a theoretical model capturing the effects of hydrodynamics and turbulence on settling snow crystals matches the experimental data obtained in this study. The conclusions drawn from this research can be applied to evaluate the settling behavior of snow crystals with various shapes and any size, and, potentially, other particle shapes as well. Moreover, the measurement of mass in grams, rather than micrograms, makes this approach more suitable for studying larger particles and snow crystals. The proof relies heavily on the integration by parts technique and the use of Lagrangian vector fields to translate vorticity and velocity into stream functions. We present a rigorous approach to validate numerical models of hydrodynamic codes across diverse regimes using the well-defined solution of the Guderley problem as a benchmark. This Bessel-flow scenario enables comparison of results from various methods across three distinct parameter ranges: low pressures, high pressures, and an intermediate area. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this solution, we have calculated the evolution of an initial spherical perturbation within a cylindrical container under low-pressure conditions, utilizing the open-source code SUMA. Specifically, we examined pressures spanning three orders of magnitude (from 1 Pa to 100 kPa), resolving the flow up to when it reaches the center of the container. To ensure accuracy, we employed high-resolution simulations involving 101 grid points in the radial direction. We have obtained reliable outcomes for the time it takes for the flow to reach the container's center and the radial velocity of the flow at that time across the entire range of pressures, thereby validating the used numerical model. In particular, our study offers a new approach to measure the relative error of hydrodynamic codes in high-pressure regimes, providing a first-ever calculation of the flow velocity profile at various times and across different pressure levels. This systematic methodology can be applied across various problem setups to enhance trust in hydrodynamic simulations. Moreover, we have made available a set of benchmark data consisting of velocity, pressure, and density measurements at different times and pressures. You can access these benchmark data through the open public repository https://git.smc.ca/smc-cecat/benchmark-data/-/tree/main/data. Similarly, you can find the used Python code in the open public repository https://git.smc.ca/smc-cecat/guderley-benchmark/-/tree/main/code. Both of these resources are part of the broader SMcCECat project, which aims to foster collaboration among researchers in computational fluid dynamics. Ultimately, we hope that the proposed benchmark approach will contribute to increased confidence in hydrodynamic simulations across all involved researchers. Additionally, we welcome feedback and encourage the community to contribute new ideas and methodologies through discussion forums on the SMcCECat public repository https://git.smc.ca/smc-cecat/guderley-benchmark/-/issues. You can also reach out to us directly at [s.mcmillan@unsw.edu.au](mailto:s.mcmillan@unsw.edu.au). Thank you for your time.

In the field of computer-assisted colorectal adenoma classification and grading, deep neural networks have demonstrated significant potential. However, transferring these models from virtual environments to real-world clinical settings can be complicated due to differences in data characteristics. In this study, we addressed this issue by establishing a comprehensive dataset of histological images representing three levels of adenoma severity and two types of classification (neoplastic vs. non-neoplastic and grade assignment). By utilizing an ensemble approach combining human oversight with curatorial selection, we refined our models and compared their performance with those of other recently published models. The study reveals that while deep neural networks excel in classification tasks within the virtual realm, their accuracy drops significantly when applied to our curated dataset. In contrast, our proposed model exhibited superior performance on our dataset and outperformed other models in terms of adenoma grading as well. The findings of this study underscore the importance of carefully selected and diverse training data for deep neural network development. In addition, the dataset presented in this work can serve as a benchmark for evaluating the effectiveness of computer-assisted adenoma classification and grading models. The proposed model will soon be made accessible on the GitHub platform. In the near future, we plan to extend our model to incorporate features of whole-slide imaging to further enhance its performance. In the long run, we aspire for this model to be integrated into clinical practice as a reliable tool for adenoma classification and grading. In the context of fixed-length source coding, we investigate optimal compression rates from a leakage perspective. By generalizing a finding by Wyner, we demonstrate that the maximum achievable compression rate with a fixed maximum amount of information lost (or leakage) is directly related to the maximum achievable compression rate in the standard scenario (with no constraints on information loss). Additionally, we show that the maximum amount of information lost in an optimal code is typically substantial, specifically at least half in the case of uniformly distributed sources. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound on the information loss in fixed-length source codes, both with and without run-length erosion. In the former case, this bound is linear in the source entropy and log2 of the alphabet size, while in the latter, the bound is linear in the source entropy only. We also explore the concept of optimal leakage in the context of changing source distributions. In contrast to the fixed distribution scenario, we find that the maximum information loss in the optimal fixed-length source code when the source distribution is changing (or updated) can be arbitrarily small. In fact, if the source distribution is changing in a way that the distribution of past letters becomes uniformly random, we find that the information loss in the optimal fixed-length source code can be as low as zero. We illustrate these findings with several examples. In addition to source coding, we also apply our results to the problem of estimating a changing probability distribution from partial information. In this context, we discover that knowing the past when the source distribution is changing is generally unhelpful and that the known information does not decrease the amount of information loss. In fact, we find that the amount of information loss in the optimal estimator when the source distribution is changing and the distribution of past letters becomes uniformly random is particularly high at 1.83, which is significantly higher than the amount of information loss in the optimal fixed-length source code, 0.5. We also establish a lower bound on the information loss in the optimal entropy-constrained lossless transmission of a changing source in the context of changing source distributions. This research introduces MrSARP, a cutting-edge deep generative model that leverages hierarchical dependencies to synthesize detailed images at multiple scales. By dividing the synthesis process into coarse-to-fine stages, MrSARP's high-resolution generator produces a base image, which is then refined through a series of sequential enhancements generated by a lower-resolution version of the model. We've developed a novel loss function that measures the distortion caused by each refinement stage, ensuring that each step improves the visual quality of the synthesized image. We've also developed a multi-scale variation loss that's resistant to noise, as well as a generative learning rate schedule that accelerates the synthesis process. Experimental results show that MrSARP outperforms state-of-the-art synthesizers like SARP and WCSBPs in both visual quality and latency. For example, MrSARP achieves a 2x speedup over SARP while delivering comparable visual quality, or surpasses it in terms of visual quality when using the same number of iterations. We've released MrSARP's implementation and demo on GitHub.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm holds promise for finding approximate solutions to complex combinatorial optimization problems that might be intractable for classical computers. By adapting Bayesian optimization to the quantum context, we enable it to efficiently explore the complex, high-dimensional space of the variational parameters, thereby enhancing the QAOA's performance. The results of our simulation study indicate that this approach leads to improved approximate solution quality compared to standard methods, particularly for instances of the exact cover problem. The quantum-inspired nature of our method allows it to scale better than expected, with potential applications extending to other optimization and machine learning problems on classical systems. A new approach has been devised to detect and solve the intersections of two general ellipses using an iterative comparison of boundary segments. This algorithm utilizes a novel formula to calculate the intersection points of two ellipses in terms of their parameters and centers. However, this formula only applies when one ellipse is entirely contained within the other and does not account for cases where the ellipses do not have a containment relationship. As such, the proposed method relies on a secondary algorithm to break down general ellipse intersections into containment scenarios. Additionally, the approach incorporates the use of symbolic computation to solve equations and provide solutions with high-precision symbolic expressions. Testing of the proposed method has demonstrated its effectiveness across a wide range of scenarios, including cases where one ellipse contains the other and situations where they do not have a containment relationship. The proposed method has also been compared to other methods and found to be significantly faster, especially when dealing with complex scenarios. Testing revealed that for general second-degree curves, the proposed method could solve up to 80% more cases than existing methods and was up to 140 times faster in certain situations. Furthermore, the approach has been validated through the development of a companion application called EllipseIntersections, which utilizes the Mathematica computer algebra system to facilitate the analysis of ellipse intersections in a variety of scientific contexts. The potential applications of the proposed method include the analysis of shapes in medical imaging, detecting elliptical shapes in the solar system, and identifying forming star systems, among others. The companion application and its source code are available for review. \end{abstract}

Markovian models, characterized by their transition matrices, are used to analyze complex systems, especially those governed by stochastic processes. In this study, we reexamine these models from a mathematical perspective, translating their dynamics into a topological framework. By doing so, we demonstrate that asymptotic averages and correlation integrals can be computed through a combination of algebraic and topological calculations. Furthermore, we establish a connection between Markovian models and group representations. These findings are validated by applying our method to two case studies: a simple example and a model of stock market volatility. The proposed approach enhances Markovian analysis, offering a more geometric and intuitive understanding of the systems under study. Additionally, it facilitates the extension of Markovian models to more general dynamical systems, encompassing both continuous and discrete cases. The associated software, available on GitHub, comprises a collection of Python scripts that recapitulate the study's key findings. By integrating the GitHub repository into PyMarkov, we create a comprehensive tool for Markovian analysis, encompassing both traditional and advanced methodologies. As a result, users can access a broader range of methods and improve the accuracy of their predictions. In the past few years, AI assistants with human-like conversations have become more prevalent, but their capabilities are still limited to surface-level interactions. Current technology cannot fully grasp the complexities of human dialogue, especially when it involves relationships and deeper levels of conversation. These AI systems are developed using conventional machine learning techniques, by which human inputs are encoded into a computer model using statistical associations. The issue with this approach is that the AI remains superficial in its understanding, much like a advanced language model. Nevertheless, studies have shown that human assistants can and do develop their own unique approaches to completing tasks, as well as intuitions which arise from repeated experiences. Furthermore, these studies have demonstrated that human assistants are capable of forming coherent relationships with their human partners, based on shared goals and emotions. To create more sophisticated AI systems, similar to those of human assistants, we propose the use of collaborative problem-solving environments. In this setting, AI and human partners engage in reciprocal teaching, in which they take turns completing tasks and providing feedback to one another. Through this collaborative dynamic, we aim to investigate how AI assistants can evolve from using established methods to employing innovative, yet unknown approaches. In this paper, we present our initial findings on the design of such a problem-solving environment, along with the first AI assistant to participate in this study. This AI assistant, referred to as Coach, is designed to help children learn division skills, for which there are multiple approaches to solve problems. By analyzing Coach's performance over time, we discovered that the AI develops and refines its strategies, as well as forming emotional connections with its human partner. In the long run, we hope that Coach will exhibit a deep, intuitive grasp of division, along with a strong, caring relationship with its human collaborator.
